speechtext: Mr. E. LAPOINTE (Kamouraska) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 49, to amend the Exchequer Court Act. .
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to amend section 20 of the Exchequer Court Act, which gives jurisdiction to the Exchequer Court to entertain certain claims against the Crown. Subsection (c) of section 20 reads:
Every claim against the Crown arising out of any death or injury to the person or to property on any public work, resulting from the negligence of any officer or servant of the Crown, while acting within the scope of his duties or employment.
As you are aware, Sir, the Crown is not liable for any wrong committed by its servants except when its liability is so provided by statute; and it has been decided by the Supreme Court of Canada, in two or three instances, especially last year in the case of Piggotts vs. the .Crown, that no claim can be entertained for an accident arising on a public work if the property or the person injured were not on the public work itself. For instance, in the case which I have just mentioned, the owner of a dock which had been destroyed through an explosion of dynamite on a Government wharf was denied all claim to compensation because his dock was on an adjoining property instead of being on the Government property itself. Judges of the Supreme Court have stated especially that the section as it stands constitutes a stupid enactment, and that justice has often been denied thereby. The amendment I propose is to insert the words "on any public work" after the words "while acting," so that the subsection will read:
Every claim against the Crown arising out of any death or injury to the person or to property on any public work, resulting from the negligence of any officer or servant of the Crown, while acting on any public work within the scope of his duties or employment.

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
The consideration of the proposed motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) for the Committee of Ways and Means, and the amendment of Mr. Turriff thereto, was resumed from Thursday, May 10.
Mr.W. F. CARROLL (South Cape Breton): Although the debate on the Budget has been somewhat extended, I desire to make a few remarks on certain features of it. From many standpoints the Budget is very satisfactory, and perhaps the most satisfactory feature in connection with it has been the.splendid response which has been made by the people of Canada to the domestic loans which were floated by the Department of Finance. I think some $350,000,000 was contributed by the people of Canada to these war loans, and that speaks well, I think, not only for the generosity of our people but for their patriotism also, and augurs well for what I conceive to be the policy that should be followed by future governments in this country in placing loans. I believe that we should continue in the future to try and meet our indebtedness by domestic loans, as that will keep the money in this country, and give to those of our people who may have money to loan the advantage of a rate of interest which hitherto has been offered to foreign countries.
Free wheat has been a live issue in this country for very many years. It was a very

live issue during the reciprocity campaign of 1911, and I am happy to say that although on that occasion there was a distinct party cleavage on the question, to-day the people of Canada, irrespective of political creed and affiliations, have come to realize that free wheat is a good thing. To-day it is no longer a matter of theory but an actual fact, and probably the Government's policy in this regard will be perpetuated. The Government are responsible for the statement that free wheat has been brought down as a war measure, but I think the people of this country will be hard to convince that such is the case. If it was a war measure, why was it postponed until the third year of the war? If free wheat were a necessity during war time, it should have been given a little earlier, say two years ago. To my mind it is simply a death-bed repentance on the part of the Government: they are endeavouring to fulfil their obligations to this country, especially to the people of the West.
Another feature of the Budget which has my most hearty approval is the taxation of war profits and other profits. I think this is a step in the right direction. Notwithstanding the fact that we may look for a speedy termination of the war, I trust that this Government or any other Government that may succeed it will continue to raise money by taxation of exorbitant profits arising not only out of war business but in any other business. If I have any criticism to make in regard to that feature of the Budget, it is that the Finance Minister has not gone far enough; he should have made the percentage a little higher. If we may judge from the circumstances and facts surrounding this feature of the Budget, the Government look on taxation of profits as merely a temporary expedient, and when the war is over they will probably resort to the ordinary taxation methods. Personally, I do not think they should do so. I think that we should look for a decrease in the tariff in the future, and if we are to have a low tariff it will be necessary to raise the new revenue by taxation of profits.
I am sure the people of this country will condemn the Minister of Finance for not introducing an income tax. The Finance Minister tells us that an income tax would be unworkable in Canada at the present time, and I have no doubt there would be many difficulties in the way of raising income tax in Canada at the present time. But difficulties will arise in all reforms of this nature. Governments must expect difficulties, and must face them in no cowardly

fashion. They had difficulties in Great Britain, no doubt, when income tax was introduced there years ago, and they had similar difficulties in the United States, and certainly the difficulties the United States had to face about a hundred years ago, when income tax was introduced there, were quite as great if not greater than the difficulties we should have to face at the present time. The Minister of Finance says an income tax should not be resorted to by the Government until the necessity becomes clearly and unmistakably apparent. Well, Sir, if ever there was a time in this country when the necessity for an income tax was unmistakably apparent, it is now when we need such a large revenue to meet our obligations. If I am correct in assuming that taxation of profits is merely a temporary measure, then we must look to some others means of taxation in this country for the future.
And I do not know any more expedient means of taxation than the income tax. Many people say that this system would be unfair to the persons who have small incomes, especially with the prices of necessaries so high as at present. That depends on how the tax is levied. It would be unfair to put a high income tax on the man whose income is only $1,000, but any man who has an income of $3,000 or upwards could well afford to pay an income tax. But these are not the only persons who would be affected. The income tax would raise revenues from the people who now are not touched at all by any form of special war tax, the half-millionaires, millionaires, multi-millionaires, who derive large incomes from money invested in various channels where it is now untaxed. I hope that when the next Budget comes down the foundation will be laid for an income tax system for Canada. Though the people of Canada have contributed $350,000,000 towards war expenditure by domestic loan, and $40,000,000 for patriotic purposes, yet the time is coming when the country will have to face, unaided by these special contributions, very large expenditures, and we who hope for a downward move in the tariff must look for other means .of raising public revenue; and I say that the only legitimate other means in sight is that of an income tax.
Many hon. members who have taken part in this debate have congratulated the Minister of Finance on the large revenues which he was able to report in his Budget. They have congratulated him
also on the fact that the value of our exports is greatly in excess of the value of our imports. Well, this may be a matter of congratulation or it may not. If we were sending $100,000,000 out to pay interest on our public debt, that would appear as an export, but it would not be a matter on which Canada should be congratulated. The system of domestic loans, if it were extended, would mean a smaller amount of interest paid outside our own borders, and this would show in the form of a relatively smaller export of goods. In this sense, a reduction of exports may be a sign of prosperity and of sound finance.
We have been asked to practise thrift and economy. The natural presumption is that those who call upon others to practise thrift are practising it themselves. There is an old saying that charity begins at home, and the Minister of Finance and hon. members of this House may be reminded by those to whom they give such good advice that thrift is like charity in this respect. I am not in a position, I am sorry to say, to declare that the Government has taken the lead in the matter of thrift and economy. Consider, for instance, the increases in expenditures by the Dominion. I have compared the figures for 1911 with those of 1915, and they work out as follows:

It will be noticed that there is an increase of 50 per cent in the expenses on account of immigration. If there is any one branch of government of which it may be said more than any other that its expenditure should not have increased, it is the Immigration Branch, and, indeed, the whole Department of the Interior. I shall refer later on to the matter of the exodus and shall show by conclusive figures that more people are leaving this country than are coming in. Why the expenditure of the Immigration Branch should increase 50 *

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
per cent in four years under such conditions is more than I can understand. As to the increase in expenditure in the Mounted Police, I do not know whether that takes in the police expenditure of the West or not. If not, then as the Mounted Police can hardly be the necessity they have been in the past, the expenditure ought to be going down instead of going up. There is an increase of 12 per cent even in the expenditure on the Yukon. This is another instance which goes to prove that this Government is not practising business economy but is rather taking the other course. For in the Yukon-and I am making no reflection on that country-there should not be the same burden of expense upon the Dominion treasury that there formerly was, because it is well known that the population of the territory has declined very much indeed. Besides the department I have named there are Dominion Lands, Railways and Canals, Weights and Measures. There has been a very great increase in the Militia Department. Of course it has been necessary greatly to increase the number of employees in that department. I shall have something to say about that later on.
But here is a Government that is telling the people that they should practise thrift and economy. Of course, the Minister of Finance is only doing his duty when he gives that advice. I think that the Government which gives that advice-gratuitous advice-should certainly make some attempt to practice the virtue that it commends to the attention of others. But, until the contrary is shown me, I am compelled to believe that the Government is very far from practising thrift. The hon. member for St. Antoine, Montreal (Sir Herbert Ames), I think it was, made the statement in this House that the appointment of additional employees is discouraged, as well as any increase of salaries.
While the appointment of additional employees should be discouraged, nevertheless the appointment of additional employees is going on. I had it a day or two ago, on what I consider to be fairly reliable authority, that the hon. the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Roche) during the present year has appointed 400 new employees in the Forestry Branch of hie department. While the hon. gentleman says new appointments are being discouraged, new appointments, nevertheless are being made. In regard to the statement of the hon. member that the advancement of salaries should be discouraged, I desire to say that if there ever was a time when the salaries of low paid officials,

either in the employment of the Government, or of corporations, or of private concerns, should be advanced, it is the present. I do not think it is necessary to extend that argument farther than to say that the prices of commodities, of the necessities of life, have gone on increasing until in some cases they have advanced 100 per cent, while the average increase is 45 per cent. In view of that fact, if there ever was a time when not only the Government of this country, but all the employers of labour should advance the salaries of their servants, that time is the present. Therefore, I do not agree with the hon. member for Montreal, St. Antoine, when he makes the statement.
As far as the Militia Department is concerned, before the war, that department had 103 employees, and since the war it has 2,078. I would not say that these employees are not necessary. Since the war the Separation Allowance and Assigned Pay Branch has been established and the employees number 604; the Records Office is also a new branch, with 634 employees; the Estates Branch is a new branch with 31 employees; the Paymaster Casualties Branch has 41 employees; the Audit Branch, 5; the Record Branch, 48; and the Deputy Chief Censor's Branch, 8. These are all new branches and there is reason for the appointment of these employees. But in the other departments, where business has not increased, possibly twith the exception of the Customs Department, I can-not see the necessity of the very large number of new employees who have been added to the staffs of these departments.
The hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) and the Government have been congratulated by their friends and others because of the good times which prevail at present. There is i.o doubt that, compared with the years 1912 to 1914, there are good times in this country, but I do not think that the Government of the day should take very much credit to themselves for having brought about these good times. During the years from 1912 to 1914 Canada faced a very serious situation. Factories were closed down and thousands of men and women were out of employment and walking our streets. Then the war came and the munition factories grew up. It is a good thing, and the people are to be congratulated upon the fact that to-day they are able to turn out millions and millions of tons of war munitions with which to fight the common enemy. That is all very well, but the situation, as far as prosperity

is concerned, arises alone and altogether from the fact that these large industries have sprung up. They are a blessing, therefore, but as far as the rest of the country is concerned, as far as our ordinary industries and manufactories are concerned, outside of those which are manufacturing the necessities of war, the country is in no better position, it is not in as good a position as it was in 1910. As a matter of fact, it is in a worse position. The labouring man has a harder time to exist, a harder time to live, a more difficult task not only to provide for himself, but to fulfil his obliga

 lions to his children and those dependent on him. I know that is true in the part of the country from which I come. While it pleases the hon. the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) to say that there is no distress in this country, I say that there is a large measure of distress due to the exorbitant prices which are being asked for the necessities of life. If the Government is to be congratulated on the fact that we have good times, I say that is true to a certain extent, but that it is as false as false can be to a still greater extent. The Minister of Labour the other evening criticised us on this side of the House for daring to say anything which would reflect in any way upon his department, or upon the manner in which he was conducting, or misconducting, that department. We, on this side of the House, as hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House representing constituencies, like to voice the grievance of the people in these constituencies, and the greatest grievance we have to voice in this House at the present time arises from the fact that the prices of foodstuffs have 'been allowed to soar so high that to-day it is practically impossible for the ordinary labourer to provide for the actual and bare necessities of life. That is not an exaggerated yarn. Any hon. gentleman who will take the time to go into this question must come to the same conclusion. The cost of labour has not gone up very much. In our own part of the country it has gone up perhaps fifteen or twenty per cent and I am looking to a still further increa.-o. but when we look around and find that the cost of living has gone up 45 per cent we see that the people are suffering an actual hardship in the effort to sustain themselves and their families. A man who was getting $2 a day two years ago is perhaps getting $2.20 at the present time. How far will that go towards maintaining a large family?
When the Minister of Labour says there . is no distress he does not know this country, he does not take the trouble to know it and I am afraid he does not take the trouble to investigate the facts in connection with the cost of living. He tells us, of course, that he did certain things, that he was responsible for the passing of the Order in Council by which the excessive cost of foodstuffs, and other commodities, could be investigated. He tells us of the sleepless days and nights he has spent over this matter. He makes two speeches in this House in the last two weeks, on this important question, one a. duplicate of the other, but while all this is going on, while the minister is taking credit for having succeeded in passing this Order in Council, and while it takes two speeches to try to satisfy the people that he is doing something, what consequences are flowing from that Order in Council and from what the Minister of Labour has done? The price of foodstuffs is still soaring. Can the Minister of Labour point to one single commodity the price of which has not been raised in the last two years? Can the minister point to one commodity the price of which has been decreased through the Order in Council which he succeeded in passing? That is a fair test. Can the minister show that the price of one of the necessities of life, which an ordinary family has to use, has decreased through his labours -or through his Order in Council?
He cannot, and that is the test of the efficiency of the Order in Council which the Minister of Labour has passed. It reminds me of a friend of mine who was speaking of a neighbour and who said that he had a large supply of very inaccurate knowledge. There may be this difference between my friend's neighbour and the Minister of Labour, that while my friend's neighbour had a large amount of information of a very inaccurate kind, the Minister of Labour apparently has no information at all, and, further than that, hits activities are misdirected, and his labours are useless, because if he is unable to point out any good that has come of these labours, then I say they are misdirected and useless and a waste of time. Two years ago, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cock-shutt), who is a valued member of the other side of the House and who always takes an active interest in public affairs, introduced a resolution in this House warning the Government and calling upon them to give some attention to the price of food-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
stuffs in Canada. Everybody who had anything to do with either the commercial or political life of this country knew that the price of foodstuffs was bound to increase during war time. I had the pleasure at that time of supporting the resolution as warmly as I possibly could. I suggested then, as I think the hon. member for Brantford suggested, that this Government should take certain control of foodstuffs, that they should appoint a food controller who would be keen and alive to his job, who would go about the country investigating, and at whose instance the Government would place certain maximum prices upon foodstuffs. The Government did not heed the warning. I remember quite well that the Prime Minister at that time said it would be an impossibility; it would be running against a rock of Gibralter; it would interfere with the commerce of this country The Australian people did not think so. The result is that to-day, as the hon. member for Brantford foretold, living is almost an impossibility to the ordinary men; and yet the Minister of Labour says there is no distress in this country, and he promulgates an Orderin Council whose affect has been nil

it has accomplished absolutely no good. If I am wrong in this statement, I should like to be put right, and to have it pointed out to me in what direction this Order in Council has made good. Has the work that has been done in connection with this Order in Council reduced 'by one iota the price of any foodstuff or other commodity that it was intended to affect?
The Order in Council is rather extended, and I shall not read it to the House. It provides a method by which certain things may be investigated. For example, it provides a method by which the council of a municipality, a town council for instance, may investigate the prices of commodities in its immediate neighbourhood. I pointed out to the Minister of Labour the other day that this was a most absurd proposal in many instances. In our own province, foT example, we have municipal councils covering in some cases hundreds of miles of territory. They meet once a year, I think in February, in some municipalities twice a year, in February and April. If the people of those municipalities have to wait for a whole year in order to place before the council of the municipality any grievance that they may have as to existing high prices of commodities in their neighbourhood, you can see what the value of the Order in Council is as regards those locali-

ties. In cities and towns that is overcome by the fact that councils meet once a week at least, in some places more frequently. That is one instance. But why did the Minister of Labour, apart from that phase of the question, place the onus upon the councils of municipalities? Why did he not himself tackle this subject? He is not a very busy man; his department are not very busy people. Why did they not tackle this proposal themselves? The retail merchants of this country-and I think I am voicing the sentiment of the great bulk of the people when I say this-are not responsible for the high prices of the commodities which they sell. As a matter of fact, I know of retailers who are selling below the price they are paying to wholesalers in order to accommodate, in some small measure, those who deal with them. In many parts of this country we have no large wholesalers. In the town from which I come, I do not think we have any wholesalers. If then we find that the price of flour is enormously high and we want our town council to investigate, where are they to investigate that question? They know quite well that the retail merchants are not making the profits on flour that they made several years ago, and they are allowed to investigate only those matters within their own jurisdiction. We have no wholesale dealers within our jurisdiction. What is our town council to do? They cannot go to Montreal, they cannot call upon the wholesaler in Montreal, Toronto or Halifax to appear before them and show cause why the price of flour is so high, because these people are outside the jurisdiction of that council. Surely the Minister of Labour and the Government can see that in those cases the Order in Council is absolutely useless. In ordinary times an Order in Council which would require, first, that the Minister should investigate, second, that thd town council or council of the municipality should investigate, and then that the report of this town or municipal council's investigation should be sent back to the Minister who would then confer with the municipalities, and the municipalities would then refer the matter to the Attorney General of the province, surely that would not be the way to deal-I might say dally-with a question of primary importance in this country, as the high price of food has been for the last year, yes for the last two years.
I am not ene of those who think that every other country is better than Canada, or that every other country is better governed than Canada. I believe that we have

the greatest country in the world and one of the best governed, irrespective of what political party controls the political destinies of the country for the time being; but in the matter of controlling food prices, I think we lag behind all our Allies, for every one of them has tackled this subject in a practical way, and has done something to retard what I may call the awful increase in the cost of the commodities of life. This Government is the only one that has failed in this respect, and I think it should be severely criticised and brought to task for its lack of action. I hope the criticism which has been made on this question, if it will not waken up the Minister of Labour, will at least waken up the other members of the Government and make them alive to the fact that they are face to face with a very critical situation in Canada, the most critical in our history since Confederation.
The Minister of Labour, in two speeches of two hours' duration, tells us that through the joint labours of the Labour Department and the labouring people of Canada this Order in Council was drawn up. I repeat that if he or any member of the Government, or any man in this country can show us any good that has come from this Order in Council I shall be the first to bless him. But the good is apparently not there, because, although the Order in Council has been in existence several months, the rise in the price of the necessities of life during that time has been marvellous. Some of the other members of the Government should tackle this question in a live way. If they do they will have the blessing of the people, and I can assure the Minister of Finance that he will have my blessing, however much that may be worth.
The criticism which has been directed against the Government has not all come from this side of the House. The most.cut-ting criticism that I heard in this House against the attitude of the Government on the question of the high cost of living.came from a gentleman who occupies a seat on the other side. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) a few nights ago said:-
Every country that professes to have a government has taken steps to control food prices.
No hon. gentleman on this side of the House made any such severe criticism as that.
It is not only the Liberal press which is criticising the Government in this respect. I picked up yesterday the Halifax Herald of May 12, 1917, which is the political organ
of the Conservative party in the province of Nova Scotia. It quotes an advertisement appearing in the Winnipeg Tribune concerning the high price of flour in Winnipeg at that time, $14.50 a barrel, and, in the editorial comment, it says:-
We appreciate the difficulties under which the members of the government have labored, and which still confront them in the prosecution of a great task. It is safe to say that no government in the history of Canada has accomplished more than the present Administration. The magnitude of the task, the well-nigh overwhelming nature of the crisis which suddenly confronted Canada in August, 1914 can scarcely be estimated, and the results achieved are universally recognized as being magnificent.
We have no wish to harass the government, but it is our belief that the time is now fully ripe for the Administration at Ottawa to deal firmly and speedily with the question of the alleged hoarding of food supplies.
In every nation, and every community, there are unfortunately a certain class of individuals who are quick to seize upon any opportunity which a crisis may afford for the sole and selfish purpose of enriching themselves at the expense of their fellows. The present food situation has been readily taken advantage of by unscrupulous food speculators to hold up various food commodities thus artificially inflating the price, the burden of which obviously falls on the masses. Such a course of action is shamefully unpatriotic, and certainly not worthy of any Britisher. Letters of protest in the press, strong invective poured forth in some platform utterance are utterly powerless to touch either the conscience or the manhood of the food-hoarder whose only god is GAIN. The strong arm of the government is alone capable of dealing with this problem in an effective manner.
At this present hour in Halifax the price of flour has soared to over $17 per barrel; potatoes cannot be purchased under 70 cents per peck; it is therefore not to be wondered at that rumours are current to the effect that Nova Scotia itself is not wholly free from the grasping hand of the food speculator. We think it is high time to call-Halt!
This is the opinion of a Conservative organ in the province of Nova Scotia.
The labour organizations of Canada have taken up this question. They have passed resolutions-copies of which, I dare say, are now in the hands of the Government- calling for speedy action. The Halifax District Trades and Labour Council has endorsed a resolution adopted by the Sydney Trades and Labour Council with reference to Government control of food. The latter part of the resolution reads:-
Be it therefore resolved, that the executive council ask for Government control of all foodstuffs until it is positively ascertained that our domestic needs are fully priTvided for and the cost of living reduced to normal conditions.

I said a few moments ago that there was no apparent reason why the expenditure of the immigration Branch of the Department of the Interior should have increased about 50 per cent during the period from 1912 to 1915. When hon. gentlemen are told that an actual exodus of people is taking place from our country, they have food for reflection, and they are impelled to give some thought to the reasons why the expenditure in connection with immigration should be so large. I shall not go to the political press for the figures which I am going to give. The following paragraph from the April number of the Labour Gazette may very profitably engage t'he attention of the Department of the Interior:
Of persons other than citizens of the United States, 1.043 left the United States in February, 1917, to take up permanent residence in British North America, as compared with 1,206 in January, 1917. On the other hand, 7,304 persons, other than citizens of the United States, departed from British North America in February, 1917, to take up permanent residence in the United States, as compared with 10,557 in January, 1917, indicating for British North America an outward balance of 6,261 in February of this class of persons as compared with an outward balance of 9.351 in January, 1917.
So that during the months of January and February of this year, there was, not taking into account American citizens, an outward balance of 15,612 persons. That does not indicate that there is that condition in this c.ountry which the Minister of Finance would lead us to believe. If the conditions were similar to those which prevailed before 1912, the figures would not be such as they are, because in that year the inward balance was far in the preponderance.
Another thing which the Immigration Branch of the Department of the Interior should take steps to inform itself about is what kind of people are going out, -where the exodus is greatest and what is its cause. Are these people 'going out to escape military service? I do not think that they could be going out at that time to escape military service, because there was no conscription.

Are they going out because of the fear of conscription in the future? I do not think that they are, because in the United States they are nearer to conscription than we are in Canada. The Government should obtain full information concerning this exodus, and should find out what kind of people are coming into the country and replacing those who have gone away. With regard to the Budget, that is all I have to say.
On reading Hansard of May 8, I was personally aggrieved to see some references made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) concerning the right hon. gentleman who leads His Majesty's loyal Opposition in this House. Had those words come from the lips of the hon. member for East Simcoe (Mr. W. H. Bennett), I do not think I would pay very much attention to them; but as they come from a gentleman who for half an hour scored hon. members on this side Of the House for their narrowness and their bigotry, I think some attention should be paid to them. This is what the hon. member for Frontenac is reported in Hansard to have said on May 8, page 1269:
I have not great admiration for a leader who posed as a man desiring interprovincial amity and concord, and has encouraged his compatriots to the verge of revolution. Nor do I admire a leader who said that he would not seek to open the doors of office with a bloody key, and has smiled approval on tactics which have encouraged the enemy, retarded enlistment, and were intended solely to serve party ends.
In a time like this, when the people of this whole Empire are doing their utmost to keep the Union Jack floating, and to be in a position in the future to sing that song we are all so fond of-" Britannia Rules the Waves;" when Canadian families have been giving of their resources and of their blood to ensure that in the future the Union Jack shall fly as freely as it has done in the past, it is wrong that a right hon. gentleman who has led a political party successfully for some twenty-one years should be pointed out and painted to this country practically as a rebel, and that the intimation should be thrown out to the people of Canada by an hon. member, that the conduct of my right hon. leader has encouraged the enemy	and retarded	enlistment, and that he has encouraged his compatriots-I	presume that	refers to the French Canadians-to the verge of revolution. Those are generalities and I challenge the hon. member for Frontenac to attempt, in any future utterances which he may care to make in this House, to prove

by one fact o,r by one utterance, the statement that he has made. It is high time that the hon. member (Mr. Edwards) should realize that this Empire is engaged in a serious war; that we are in the greatest crisis in which we have ever found ourselves, and that those sentiments to which he gave utterance the other day are not calculated to heal any sores that at the present time may be running in this country, but are calculated, on the contrary, to mark him as a man of very narrow vision, of very narrow ideals, and as a man who is attempting for political purposes to keep these sores open. We on this side of the House-and I do not think it should be necessary to reiterate this-are as loyal to the cause for which many of our friends have shed their blood as is the hon. member, and with the exception of the hon. member for Frontenac and the hon. member for East Simcoe who charged me with running away in order to escape the bullets of the enemy and with returning to Canada unscarred, there are few on the other side who would give utterance to such sentiments. We want it known in this country that we have a leader who, from the moment the gauntlet was thrown down by Germany -and taken up by Great Britain, has done his utmost to fulfil the duty that is his by virtue of his being leader of the Opposition. Had he not done that and had rve not confidence in him that he was doing his duty, he would not be our leader to-day; we would see to that ourselves. We have every confidence in the loyalty, not to speak of the integrity, of the right hon. gentleman who has successfully led the Liberal party for upwards of twenty-one years. Any man who introduces such questions and who tries to cast aspersions on my right hon. leader is not acting in the interest of this country at this or at any other time. maintopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with surprise to hon. gentlemen opposite praising this wonderful Budget of the Minister of Finance. In my humble judgment, the Budget is no compliment to the intelligence of the people of this country. A Budget was brought down in Great Britain a few days ago. They know they are at war in that country, especially do the rich. While the British Chancellor is taking 80 per cent of the gross war profits and raising enormous sumsj the Canadian Minister of Finance runs a small tooth comb through the fringes and raises the paltry sum of $12,500,000. It is time our rich men were making sacrifices commensurate with those of the boys in the trenches. There is a great contrast between that $12,500,000 and the twelve

thousand casualties at Vimy Ridge It is time our manufacturers disgorged. Lloyd George, at the commencement of this war, said that men and money would win the war. Canada has given over 400,000 of her brave sons to fight the battles for freedom and justice in France. And when I think of the hardships that these men have to undergo, in the trenches with water to their knees, and sometimes to theirlhips in mud, sometimes going for days and nights without food and sleep-when I think of the sacrifices these men are making on the fields of France and Flanders, and then think of the paltry sum of only twelve and a half millions taken from the wealth of this country toward the expenses of the war, I think it time that some change were made in the matter of raising money to meet war expenses. As I speak there comes to my memory instances of the sacrifices that have been made. In the principal town of the constituency I have the honour to represent are 'a number of widowed mothers. One of these mothers had two sons; both those sons went to the front and gave their lives cheerfully on behalf of this country. And the widowed mother must put in the rest of her life on $22 a month, the gift of a grateful country. Another woman lost her husband in a Canadian Northern wreck several years ago. She had three or four sons. Of these, two went to fight our battles, and they will never return. Still another woman lost two of her five sons in defence and for the maintenance of the world's freedom. When I think of these sacrifices and then of the fact that the wealthy men of Canada have given only twelve and a half million dollars, I am compelled to say that is not a square deal for the common people. And in my constituency-and I presume that the same is true of every other part of Canada-the noble women lhave worked night and day, sewing, and knitting, and raising money in every way to give to the Patriotic Fund, Red Cross, and Soldier's Aid Society. These people give every dollar in their power, and the wealthy men of Canada have been left practically untouched. In calling for volunteers to fight, we do not take the weak men; if a man is not physically sound, he is turned down. If we want men who are physically strong to fight our battles, surely it is only square to the people that we should look to the men who are strong financially to pay for the war. The Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) has told the House that the war orders last year amounted to $300,000,000. If our Minister of
Finance had taken: of war profits to anything like the same extent as in Great Britain, he would have had a great deal better showing, to make in taxation. Instead of $12,500,000, he could have shown war profits taxation of $100,000,000. Hon, gentlemen opposite have asked us how we propose to raise revenue if not by tariffs. I have. just, pointed out one way in which a large sum could be raised. Further, there is. no reason why the Finance Minister of Canada should not follow the example of Great Britain and the United States in the matter of income tax. Again, certain calculations have shown that a tax of one per cent on land values in Canada would yield large revenues. Mr. Henry Timmis, of Montreal, in a speech reported in the Montreal Herald and Daily Telegraph of March 28, 1917, estimated that the land values of Canada total $8,000,000,000-five billions; in the towns and cities and three billions in the rural districts. A tax of one per cent on this valuation would bring revenue to the amount of $80,000,000 per annum. I have already shown where the Minister of Finance could have got $100,000,000 in war taxation, and I think that my estimate is a very moderate one, for men who pretend to know say that instead of $100,000,000 he could have taken $200,000,000 from the manufacturers during the last fiscal year. Then, if he had imposed an income tax, I feel satisfied he could have raised at least $50,000,000 by that -means. I am not sure of my ground in this respect, having no means to make more than a rough calculation. The minister has financed the war from the revenues of the year just closed to the extent of $60,000,000. Now, taking all these items together-$100,,000,000	direjct war
taxes, $80,000,000 land value tax, $50,000,000 income tax and $60,000,000 surplus revenues of last year, and we have a total of $290,000,000. I submit in all fairness that if the methods I have -suggested had been adopted, we could have financed the war as we went ialong, which would have been much more -satisfactory to the Canadian -people than to balance our accounts by borrowing money, thus leaving future generations to pay the bill. Had -the Minister of Finance -the courage to follow these methods, he could have accomplished two things. In -the first place, he could have removed some tariff taxation. For instance, he might have taken the tax off agricultural implements, and this would have given a tremendous boost to production. There is no further excuse for this tax, for our manufacturers now have free entry to the United

States, of which they have taken advantage -many agricultural implements made in .Canada are now sold more cheaply in the western States than in our own country. (These patriotic gentlemen are making production easier in the United States by robbing our own farmers. Let me dwell on this point for a moment to show what the western farmer is called upon to endure. When he 'buys agricultural machinery he has to pay a duty of from 25 to 27j per cent. Let me cite my'own specific case. I bought a gasoline tractor and a separator, and, as pearly as I could figure, I paid duties amounting to $500.

We have to pay more for every thresher, binder and mower, and yet we get no more for our products than does the American farmer, and so the American farmer is given an advantage over U3 by our own laws. If the Minister of Finance could only see his way clear to adopting this method of raising the revenue, he could remove a burden from the western farmers and put them on a fair competitive basis with the American farmers. In that way he would increase the production of western Canada. Speaking from memory, we produced $600,000,000 worth of grain last year in the three western provinces. That is $600,000,000 of clean, hard-earned money and if the burden were lifted from the farmers' back and markets opened up to them to encourage settlement, there is no doubt in the world that instead of producing $600,000,000 worth of grain we could produce twice that amount in a short time
Before we get away from the war situation, et me say that the most important thing that we have to do at the present time is to wm this war. There are four essentia! things in connection with it that require organization and support. First, there is the question of our men in the trenches next the munition factories, then the farmers and producers, and lastly the transportation question. Our men in the
trenches are no good without munitions
with which to face the Germans. They can not face them for any length of time without food. Food and munitions are no good in Australia or Canada or the United States without means of transportation to get them to the men. I feel as if the Government had risen to the occasion in connection with practically everything but the finding of men to take the places of our brave soldiers who are in France. Our distinguished Prime Minister promised 500,000 men to Great Britain. He has failed so far in getting those men. I think it is up to every man on both sides of this House to do everything in his power to fulfil the Prime Minister's pledge to the British Government.
Another point I want to make while I am on this subject is that it appears to me as if this Government were centralizing the wealth of the country. Before the Prime Minister went to England he made the statement in this House that we were getting $700,000,000 worth of war orders. The Minister of Finance made the statement in Toronto that he believed after the war was over Canada would come out of it in a better financial position than that in which she was when she went into it. I 'would like to ask the Finance Minister and hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, as well as on this side, who is going to come out of this war in a better position? It is not *the' common people of the country, it is not the men who are fighting our battles, but it is the men who are making millions out of the manufacture of munitions. It has been stated that they are making from 25 to 900 per cent. I do not know what they are making, but they are certainly making large profits, and they are allowed to invest them with the Minister of Finance in the war loans, with the result that they are exempt from taxation. In this way the Government are centralizing the wealth of the country. These men are making large profits, a good deal larger than they should make, and they are investing them in Government bonds, which cannot be taxed, so that, in my judgment, the Government are centralizing the wealth of the country in the hands of probably 3,000 or. 4,000 people, which is a great mistake and a great hindrance to the progress of the country.

When hon. gentlemen are talking about financing a great part of the war as we go along, it seems to me that they are misleading the House and the country.
I would like to submit a few more figures in connection with the claim that the expenses of Government are not increasing. In the last year of the Liberal Government, 1911-12, the total disbursements were $137,142,082. In 1915-16 the expenditure of the present Government for a full year, apart from the war, was $170,317,847. If you subtract $137,142,082 from $170,317,847, you get $33,175,765 as the sum that it cost this Government during the last fiscal year to carry on the affairs of the country more than it did in 1911-12, the last year that the Liberal party had anything to do with the running of the country.
I come now to free wheat. I do not intend to dwell upon the question of free wheat to any great extent. It has been said that the farmers of western Canada are pleased to have free wheat. We are pleased to have free wheat because we have asked for it and we have fought for it. We have got it from the present Government, and we appreciate it very much. But we regret that when the Government, or the Minister of Finance, were turning a somersault they did not also give us free oats, free flax and free barley.
The Minister of Finance, when he made his last speech, mentioned the Highways Bill, and claimed that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House were against that measure. If I understand the situation, that statement of the minister is unfair. When the Highways Bill was under discussion, an amendment was moved that when any province got its allotment according to population, every other province should get its proportion on the same basis. That amendment was moved to prevent the hon. the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers) from taking power to create an organization in each of the provinces to spend that money. Wherever there was a Liberal Government in power this Government would create another -organization to spend the money, and the people of Manitoba know what the late Roblin Government did in connection with the building of rpads. In some provincial constituencies they spent as much as $90,000 to win a by-election. We do not want that to occur again.
The hon. gentleman also mentioned the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba. We appreciate very much the extension of our boundaries, but every one in western Canada knows that the territory allotted to the province of Manitoba by this Government was the same as that offered by the late Government. The amount of money paid over may have been a little larger, but the territory was the same. In extending the boundaries of Manitoba, this Government gave Ontario a five-mile strip across the northern part of our territory and a strip ten miles down the Nelson river, half a mile wide; so that Ontario owns the townsite and this strip of land across the northern territory. The amendment moved by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was to the effect that while the House favoured the extension of the boundaries of Manitoba the terms proposed were unfair and unjust to the people of Manitoba and the other provinces of the Dominion. That was the amendment moved, and for that I voted. When the Minister of Finance mentions Manitoba and what has been done for western Canada, and when hon. gentlemen cast insinuations across the floor of the House to the effect that the Opposition, when in power, did not carry out their pledges to the people, I would remind hon. gentlemen that when the present Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) was in western Canada previous to 1911, he told the people of the three western provinces that one of the first things he would do if he was returned to power would be to restore to the three western provinces their natural resources. I would remind hon. gentlemen that this pledge has never been fulfilled. I hope that it will be fulfilled in the very near future.

['I am not advocating the English method; I am advocating a common sense method which will apply to everybody equally and alike and under which the rich man will pay according to his means and the poor man will pay also according to his. The price of wheat should not be over 90 cents to $1 a bushel; to-day it is $3 a bushel. The price of flour is $16 a barrel. The minister says that the press of the country must be sustained because it is one of the necessities. If a poor man has a big family and they are crying for bread will they be satisfied with the evening paper? Does it not appeal to the minister that there are other things as well as newsprint that ought to be regulated? The minister says that the winning of the war is the one and the main thing to which we should give our attention but I cannot help thinking that when this delegation from the press came down with their stocking full of printers' ink and told him that they would knock his political head off if he did not listen to them he said: hold
on, gentlemen, 1 do not want to be disfigured that way, I will listen to you; what will you have-paper at 21 cents a pound?-all right, gentlemen, you shall have it; the manufacturer can squeal all he likes but he has got no printers' ink and he cannot hurt me very much with his tongue. I am sorry to believe these things but I leave it to the judgment of the House and the people of the country to say if there is any just reason why the price of newsprint should be fixed at 21 cents a pound, which is one cent less than it can be made for when other branches of business are left untouched. I noticed a short time ago in the Financial Times that a company making sulphite pulp were describing the profits they had made during the last year when the average price was so much; they stated what they expected to make next year when the average price was going to be so much and they ended up by saying that " our business is not affected by the price fixed for newsprint." Why should this condition exist? Why should this one branch of the industry be left so that they could boast that they could make such large profits because they were not affected by what affected another branch of the same industry? I am not jealous of other .people. I wish I could say for the minister and for the Government that they had treated the manufacturers of newsprint as they treated other branches of the industry. I think it would be to the advantage of the Government and for the publishers if that were the case. The publishers are going to suffer for it later on, because they have prevented the construction of additional plants which would have afforded the only remedy for their complaint. If they had patience for about twelve months from the time they started to make the kick, the position would have rectified itself, as there would have been such competition that they could have again dictated the prices as they had done for the past ten years. Simply because we reached a period where for a few months they had to pay an additional price, they .had not the 'foresight to see what would .happen in the future. They made their kick at the wrong time, and will be sorry .for it later on. The American publishers are sorry for it now. They started to fix the price, but they saw where they were going, and thought it best to wait and see what would happen. The Canadian Government would do well, even at this late hour, to change their position, and say to the publishers:	Let supply and demand
govern these things, it is the best regulator', "of prices on the face of the earth. And the *minister would be wise to consider well *before imposing additional war taxes on the manufacturers of this country, and see *if he cannot- find some other way of levying taxes so as not to drive capital away *and prevent its investment in Canada. We *who are here will stand it as beet we can, *but the man outside will do as the man to whom you are trying to sell bonds, who *will not buy bonds unless he has some assurance that the bonds will not be loaded down with income tax. The same thing applies to the man with money in his pocket; he will not .invest in a plant in this country unless he has some assurance that it will not be singled out and made to bear the whole burden of the war and other expenses of this country, while other men, equally able to pay, go scot free.

I presume that the reason why my hon. friend the minister made his tax in this way was because it touched the least number of people -and was most convenient.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I know that it will be a detriment to the obtaining of capital in this country for industry. I presume it would, perhaps, be unwise and also not in accord with the general feeling of the people of the country if I were to say that it would be unwise taxation to endanger the investment of capital in this country. I do not know what the minister's aim is exactly, whether he aims to make this country a pastoral country altogether, or a farming community altogether, or if his aim is to stop big business in this country. If his aim is to stop big business in this country he is going the right way about it. If it is not to stop large business in Canada he is going the wrong way about it. The financial papers, as the minister knows, are protesting, some of them very strongly, against this taxation. A man named Kelly Dickinson, writing to the Financial Times, quotes three firms which have cancelled important contracts for enlargements of plant, etc. One Montreal company abandoned as contemplated investment of an additional $1,000,000 in their business. An American firm abandoned its intention to establish a Canadian subsidiary company with an initial investment of $2,500,000. Another firm, which had contracted for a number of new lathes to replace worn out lathes, cancelled the order and decided to do the best it could with the impaired and worn out plant. So

far as I am personally concerned, I think there is no one thing that we want in this country more than capital. We cannot possibly develop the natural resources of this country without it. We hear a great many people talking, both after dinner and before, about the wonderful natural resources of Canada, hut we cannot develop them without encouraging capital to develop them. My hon. friend, I think, is discouraging capital by his peculiar legislation here. I appreciate that it is absolutely necessary to get more revenue, but why my hon. friend should relieve all the people of this country who do not have $50,000 invested in their business from paying their proportion of the revenue is more than I can comprehend or could comprehend last year when the original resolution imposing this business tax was passed.
I do not think any of these manufacturers or business men would complain about paying the additional tax if my hon. friend would only make it equitable. But he does not make it equitable; he applies it only to businesses of a certain size, and the others he does not tax at all. Again, many professional men earning very large incomes entirely escape this taxation. I do not think that is fair. Having regard to the seriousness of this war and the absolute necessity of a large revenue, every business should pay its just proportion of taxation. My hon. friend may know of many people who would object to paying the tax, but I think that the great mass of the manufacturers put in honest statements in connection with last year's taxation, and I believe that the great mass of the people carrying on businesses in which less than $50,000 is invested would also submit honest statements. I do not think it would cost the minister very much more to collect the taxes from all of these businesses than it would to collect only from those which have a capital investment of over $50,000. Yet my hon. friend this year increases the taxation on those who are earning the larger profits. As I have said, I am quite sure that if the minister would spread the taxation over a larger area, as it were, and make everybody pay a share of the taxation, there would be no unwillingness on the part of the people to assist in this way to met the huge expenditure that is being made in connection with the war.	[DOT]
I have to find fault with my hon. friends of the Government for not assisting the people during the last year. The Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Labour

had a golden opportunity, which, perhaps, will never come to them again, of rendering a very important service to the masses of the people. For instance, the Minister of Agriculture allowed it to be stated in the papers without contradiction that he had said that there were 2,000,000 bushels of potatoes in Canada more than were necessary for the ordinary consumption of the people. That was his opportunity to have seen that these potatoes were equitably distributed in those parts of the country in which they were required.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: My hon. friend's statement is not quite correct. He says that I made a certain statement and allowed it to go uncontradicted; I am prepared to stand by the statement which I made as it is reported in Hansard. What I stated was that early in March, at a conservative estimate, there was' a surplus of a million and a half bushels, and so there was. But I stated that a large number of potatoes had gone out of the country since that time, and I specifically stated the other day that that surplus did not now exist, or at all events, had greatly diminished, and that the provinces had all been advised of the facts and had taken action.

An hon. gentleman near me says that the million and a half bushels was the amount exported. As a rule, I am opposed to coercive measures on the part of a government, but that was .a time when the Government would have been justified in using coercive measures. In other words, they would have been justified in placing an embargo on the export of potatoes. I am strongly of the view that the law of supply and demand should govern such matters, but conditions arise which justify a government in going to unusual lengths. Under conditions that are exceptional, the people are the first to be considered. In our section of the country-I do not know about other sections- during the last three or four months potatoes have been out of the reach of people who are working with their hands or who are receiving small salaries. My hon. friend says that his statement was that the surplus of potatoes was only a million and a half bushels. There is no reason why he should not have grasped the opportunity of distributing those potatoes in the areas where they were required. That would have been justified, having regard to the interests of the people. If the matter was one which came under the
Labour Department, then the Minister of Labour would have been justified in taking that course. There are many other things that the Government would have been justified in doing during the last few months, but I have no wish to delay the committee;
I simply wish to put my views on record before- this measure is passed without amendment. I hope that the minister will see his way clear to enlarge this proposed legislation so as to make it just and equitable. My hon. friend says that he leaves the income tax to the provinces. He may be justified in that, to some extent; some of the provinces are adopting an income tax. I noticed the other day that the province of British Columbia proposes to have an income tax. In my opinion, this form of taxation is bound to come and we may as well face it first as last.
5 p.m. Certainly the scope of the profits tax legislation should be enlarged, because many men who have less than $50,000 invested in their business are, proportionately speaking, making more money than the men with from $50,000 to $100,000 invested. These men should pay their fair proportion of the unusually heavy expenditures which are being made during this time of war. I congratulate the country on the amount of business which is being carried on; it is an exceptional business, but the export of goods has been at an exceptionally high price. An increase in the value of import's does not necessarily represent an increase in tonnage of imports. In many instances the value of imports has doubled or trebled, whereas the tonnage has not appreciably increased. In a business with which I am connected, the tonnage of imports did not increase, while in the case of some of the imports the value was trebled.
Therefore, you cannot always judge the amount of business actually done by the total in dollars and cents of the imports and exports of this country during the last year or two. Although I have no doubt this item will pass from the committee and will become law, at the same time, I simply enter my protest against its scope not being enlarged.

Before the minister answers the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) I would like to have the minister give approximately, if he can, the revenue he anticipates from the additional taxation provided for in the resolutions before the committee. In delivering his

Budget speech, the minister, if I remember correctly, did not venture to make any estimate of the amount that would' probably be derived from this taxation, and I should like to have some idea, even if it be a rough one, of the revenue which the minister hopes to secure from this source.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Listening to my hon. friend from North Oxford, I could not help but reflect upon the Protean character of the Opposition. My hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Cruise), just a few minutes before, had been attacking the Government as a whole and myself in particular because we were not taking more money out of the manufacturers. Only the other day, as I saw by the Press, my hon. friend from Sherbrooke (Mr. MeCrea), in my absence, launched a violent .attack against me for taking too much money out of the manufacturers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: No, not the manufacturers.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, let u.s say the paper manufacturers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My right hon. friend, however, will not fail to have observed that another of his followers, the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), whom we are always glad to hear in debates of this kind, has taken the ground that the taxation is so severe that it is likely to drive capital out of the country and prevent new capital from coining in.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: The taxation is strong all around.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Does my right hon. friend object that it is strong all around? My right hon. friend is behind his usual lines of Torres Vedras. He has become so accustomed to that position that I rarely, almost never, expect to see him depart from it. He always likes to have a double policy; he likes, as they say, to play both ends against the middle. My hon. friend from North Oxford has said in the course of his remarks that this tax will be a detriment to obtaining further capital for industries, and he has made his own the articles which have appeared in the Financial Times of Montreal, violently denouncing me for introducing this excess profits tax, so that' I find myself in the position of being attacked by some hon. gentlemen opposite for not being severe enough in the taxations and by others for 
being too severe. That is a position to which we are not unaccustomed in the course of debates in this House.
My hon. friend from North Oxford, in developing his argument, stated that there is nothing in Canada we want more than capital. If we wrere in times of peace, I might not be disposed to wholly agree with him, because there might conceivably be things that we require more than capital; but on the whole I think I would have agreed to him, to this extent at all events, that capital is a great desideratum to this country; more than that, it is a necessity for its development. But this is not a time of peace; this is a time of war, and there is at least one thing which is more necessary to Canada at this time than even capital, and that is that we win this war, or do what we can to help to win this war.
Is capital not required to win this war?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I submit that what I have stated is correct.
How are you going to win the war without capital?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At this time the winning of the war is more important than the attracting of capital. If my hon. friend would like me to develop that argument a little, I am quite prepared to do so.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Go on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are in this country some industries which directly and materially assist in the prosecution of the war. They are absolutely necessary and we icould not conceivably carry on the war without them. We have derived and the Empire has derived an enormous advantage from industries in this country which have by their output contributed directly to the winning of this war. In addition to that, there are in this country other industries which contribute indirectly to the winning of the war, and those industries are also valuable to the country. There are others which contribute to the support and maintenance of the people during the war, and Wgain there are other industries which, {neither immediately nor indirectly, contribute towards the winning of the war, but which nevertheless do contribute to the financial strength of the country during [DOT]war time by exporting their products and an that way helping to create a favourable financial balance which is of advantage to the country in the winning of the war. These [DOT]might be classed as industries in a way

assisting in the winning of the war. At this time it is an important thing to Canada to secure capital for the development of industries. It by no means follows-I do n-ot say it is not desirable-that it is the most necessary thing. The most necessary thing in this country to day is to make available the man power of the country for the winning of the war, that is to say, for the replenishing of the ranks .of our expeditionary force, for the production of munitions and other supplies, including of course food-
If my hon. friend means to say that he does not require capital for that purpose, that is nonsense.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: -in order economically to develop the resources of the country so that we may the more effectually carry on the war. As to the attraction of capital, I would agree at once, that it would be a very desirable thing that capital should flow into this country. Notwithstanding the fact that we have had to impose taxation, it is desirable that capital should flow into this country provided that it 'be used for the development of our resources, for the carrying on of the war or for making us strong financially. But I say this, that if capital is going to be prevented from coming into this country by reason of taxation which is necessary in order that this country may maintain the burden of the war, we might better impose the taxation and not have the capital than have the capital and not impose the taxation. That is the position I take with respect to this matter. It is no pleasure for any Government or for any Minister of Finance to have to impose taxation; but I dp not know of any country that can carry on war without imposing taxation, nor do I know of any country that should attempt to carry on war without imposing taxation.

No one takes
exception to that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
from North Oxford
I did not take exception to anything of the kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend from North Oxford says that' this taxation will prove a detriment to obtaining capital for industries. I have taken down my hon. friend's words. He produces the Financial Times to support his argument.
He did not mean to say that he was opposing the taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He was opposing the excess profits taxation, which I have submitted to the House. Otherwise his words are meaningless.
That may be true; that is another thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does capital flow into England to-day? England is' taxed to the very bone; every industry in that country is taxed.

Does the minister think
it would do any harm if capital did flow in?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The excess profits tax in England raises $800,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: $800,000,000. That excess profits tax is severe to the last degree. Only recently has it been increased by the Chancellor of the Exchequer. If my hon. friend is right in his argument that capital will not flow into this country by reason of our excess profits tax, will capital flow into England with their excess profits tax?
They have income tax in England.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They have both excess profits tax and income tax; I want~ to make that clear, and I am glad my hon. friend has brought the point up. I have seen tax bills both with respect to income and excess profits in Great Britain, and I give you my word that on this continent we do not know what taxation means.

Nobody is fighting that.
SiT THOMAS WHITE: My hon. friend from North Oxford has brought up an article in the Financial Times condemning this excess profits tax on the ground that it would be a detriment to obtaining special capital for industry.
I read what the Financial Times said; I did not say it myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do you agree with what the Financial Times said?
Yes, I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend agrees with it. He says that the excess profits tax will have the effect of preventing capital coming into Canada, and will be a detriment to obtaining capital for industry, and on that ground he says this taxation is objectionable; in other words,

he is against it. We have at least found out my hon. friend's position on this matter. He is opposing the excess profits tax on the ground that it is too severe, that it will be a detriment to Canada's obtaining capital for industry, and will prevent capital coming into Canada. I submit to this committee that neither of those are good grounds for not imposing an excess profits tax at this time. Let us see what it amounts to. The excess profits tax which I introduced last year was limited to three years, to three yearly accounting periods expiring after December 31, 1914. Reference has beep made here this afternoon to the fact that only $12,500,000 was obtained the first year. But the first year was the year following the outbreak of war, when business was completely dislocated in this country. I stated, when introducing that taxation, that we should derive a much larger amount for the second accounting period. Now, the present taxation applies to the last accounting period; in other words, to the accounting period ending after December 31, 1916.
You are making it permanent, whereas last year it was temporary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The three-year
term is not interfered with.

I was just asking whether my hon. friend intended to make this permanent, or would it cease at the end of the war?
Sir THOMAS W'HITE: This excess profits tax applies to the last accounting period; that is to say, to the accounting period of every company which ends after December 31, 1916. The accounting periods referred to are accounting periods under the excess profits tax which I introduced last year, and which was limited in its operation to December 31, 1917. We are not extending the term.
You are not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. Let us see what we are doing. Instead of taking 25 per cent of the profits in excess of 7 per cent, which is the amount allowed incorporated companies, from 15 to 20 per cent we are taking one-half the profits, and from 20 per cent upwards 75 per cent of the profits. Now, that is -a very heavy tax; there is no question about that. It has been brought to my attention that some companies are making from 75 to 100 per cent on their capital, and, of course, the

taxation they will have to pay will be very large, but I submit that that is not the real question before the committee and the House. It is not a question of whether the tax is high, but whether it ought to be paid at this time. This is a time at which the people of this country are making immense sacrifices.

It is a time when
you should tax more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend
suggests that we should tax more. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) did not make that suggestion.
Oh yes, he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will come to that in a moment. The hon. member for North Oxford has distinctly stated that he agrees with the Financial Times that this excess profits tax will be a detriment to obtaining capital for industries in Canada. I would point out to my hon. friend from Pictou that when he suggests this taxation should be more severe, he is not in agreement with my hon. friend from North Oxford, who thinks the tax so heavy as to keep capital from coming into this country. This is a time in which the people of this country are making the greatest possible sacrifices. Men and women are sending their sons to the front. The men who have gone forward have interrupted their careers; they have left their hearth and home and everything they held most dear; they have given up everything and gone to the front, and unless what we have said from the beginning is meaningless these men are fighting for you and for me. Now in a situation such as we and all other belligerent nations are in to-day, mere money, while of great practical importance, is in reality of secondary importance. The making of profits, highly desirable in time of peace, and not undesirable, within bounds, in time of war, must take an entirely secondary place; that is the opinion, I think, of all thoughtful people in this Dominion. A mere money question becomes of secondary importance; it is of paramount importance in time of peace, hut of secondary importance in time of war. The loss of money or the taking of money by taxation is as dust in the balance compared with these other losses that are taking place in the homes of this country. I do not believe myself that a man who is making 100 per cent has any right to complain if the Government steps in and says it must have 50 or 60 per cent of their
MAY Io, 1917
profits, and I believe that public opinion will sustain this taxation measure on these grounds, even if some capital that might have come into Canada does not come in by reason of the imposition of this tax.
Let me say another thing. There is no reason *why capital seeking investment should not flow into this country to-day notwithstanding the taxation. Look at the taxation of the United States, actual and prospective. I think the business man of the United States, as one of their leading men told me over there the other day would not be deterred by this taxation measure from coming into Canada, because he is going to be pretty heavily taxed at home anyway. So that argument is not of very much weight, even from a business standpoint. I am discussing this matter at some length because it has been discussed in the press, or in a certain portion of it, and I say that the people of this country demand that men shall not be permitted to make undue profits in time of war. I say undue profits; I believe the public are quite willing that men should make reasonable profits. It has been said that men will not put forth an effort if we are going to take away 50 or 75 per cent of their excess profits. I do not believe that is so.
