I do not believe that any patriotic man will relax his efforts because the Government intends to take fifty per cent, or seventy-five per cent, of his excess profits; I have too high an opinion of the people of this country to believe it.
Why do you not tax accumulated wealth as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will come to that in a moment. The hon. gentleman always anticipates. He is the most anticipatory member we have.

But the minister
finishes without dealing with these matters.
Sir THOMAS W7HITE: I will finish all right. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) asked: what about the income of the professional man? That is a fair subject for argument. But, if we are to compare Canada with England in this matter we must bear in mind one respect in which Canada differs from England. There they have only one income tax, that imposed by the Imperial Parliament; but in this country it is possible to have three different income taxes, that of the municipality, that of the province, and that of the
Federal Government. The income tax is peculiarly within the jurisdiction of the province and is a suitable tax for the pur-jioses of the province and the municipality. In my opinion the Federal Government should not resort to an income tax until it is indispensably necessary in the national interest that it should do so. Suppose that a man is taxed on his income for the bene. fit of the municipality. He may be taxed 20 mills-two per cent. There may be a further income tax for the province. If you add to these a Federal income tax, the total impost may be very heavy. I pointed out in-the Budget speech that the incomes of the professional and salaried classes generally have not increased since the war broke out, in many cases their incomes have actually diminished. On the other hand you have the high cost of living- higher than ever before in Canada. To levy an income tax upon these people under these conditions does not seem to me just. Of course, if it becomes unavoidable, if the Dominion Government finds itself in a position where it must have an income tax, I would not hesitate to resort to it. I believe that it is quite possible, even probable if the war goes on for another year or two, that the Dominion Government may have to resort to an income tax.
Now, my hon. friend has asked why the tax has not been broadened and applied to all corporations, even those that have a capital of less than $50,000. We discussed that at length last year. I admit there is a good deal to be said in favour of that view. But there are considerations on the other side as well. In all taxes on income, there is an exemption of a greater or smaller amount. But suppose that in this case you make no exemption, and consider the case of a company with a capital of $40,000 and making seven per cent profit. That means a total profit of $2,800 for the year. Having regard to the.taxation by the municipalities, there is not a very great margin to go on in the case of these small companies. For that reason, and also for the reason that the expense of creating the staff and of collecting from these small concerns would be so great that we should probably not be further ahead by including them, we decided in favour of an exemption of corporations with a smaller capital than $50,000. That is the position taken last year, and I see n,o reason to change our views.
This brings us to another consideration concerning the income of the professional man referred to last year and also in the

present debate. The tax on corporations is a tax on excess profits. The tax on income would affect not merely professional men but those having incomes from investments, such as mortgages and securities of various kinds. Men who derive incomes from mortgages and other securities rarely net more than five or six per cent. But under the excess profits tax the profits of corporations up to seven per cent are exempted. Suppose that a man with a capital of $100,000 invests in the bonds of an industrial company. He will derive an income of $5,000 or $6,000 a year. He is still below the $7,000 which is exempted under the excess profits tax. Therefore, there is not the glaring anomaly that has been suggested in exempting the income derived from investment and amounting to less than seven per cent.
But if a man has an income of $50,000 a year from such investments, why not tax him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If we bring in an income tax, it must be general in its application. It must be remembered that under the excess profits taxation we are not taxing capital, the very principle of this measure is the taxation of profits. If profits are abnormal, it must be owing to war conditions-that is, money is being made out of the war, or notwithstanding the war. But take the case of the man with investments which yield him an income of $50,000. That would represent five per cent on an investment of $1,000,000. Now, if you have a company with a capital of $1,000,000, its annual profits would be exempted up to $70,000-that is seven per cent on its million-dollar capital.

But what would be urged is that the money in the joint stock company would give employment to a large number of men and women and would mean the circulation of money for the benefit of the community, which is not the case with the capital of the men who derive an income in the way suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The money of the individual invested may be in the very enterprise to which the hon. gentleman refers. He may be the owner of its bonds, and in that case his capital is just as much employed in keeping that industry going as is the money of the man who has contributed to its share capital.
But without risk.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not without risk. The bondholders do not always escape without risk. Now, my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) asked why we did not tax capital.

I asked why you
did not tax accumulated wealth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman said " capital " and I said I would come to that point, though he thought I would not. Now, let us see how far the hon. gentleman will go. Capital, in the sense in which he uses the term, that is, accumulated wealth, may consist of real estate, or it may consist of personal property, such as bonds and stocks. My hon. friend asks: why do you not tax that property, that capital? Well, that is arguable. The Dominion Government some day may have to extend, as I statecT in my Budget speech, the basis of taxation. My hon. friend has in mind: why do you not tax land, farms, and the real estate in towns and cities? Why do you not tax, in addition to that, the capital of those who have bonds, stocks and other securities, which are personal property? That is not the principle of this Bill, and they have not adopted that principle of taxation in any of the belligerent nations, so far as I know. They may have done so, but, if they have, it has not been drawn especially to my attention. The principle of this tax, I submit, is sound, that if there are firms, companies or businesses in Canada which in war time are making large profits, they must give a substantial portion of those profits to the Dominion Government for the purpose of assisting in carrying on the war. That is the principle. If a company has a capital of a million dollars and is not making 7 per cent, we do not tax that company, notwithstanding that it has a capital of a million dollars. I think that is just, for this reason, that that company may have a capital of a million dollars and yet it may have a thousand shareholders, each shareholder being interested only to the extent of $1,000. We know that that company is an entity, but it is made up of a thousand individual shareholders. We are not taxing that capital if they are making less than 7 per cent, but if they are making 40 or 50 per cent, we say: You are making a profit away beyond what we think you should be making in war time; you are making it out of munitions, or out of material which goes into the production of munitions, or out of supplies or other business, and you are making abnormal profits.

We say: if you make so much money as that, we propose to take part of it for the purpose of carrying on the war. That is the principle of the Bill, and even if it had the effect of preventing capital from coming into this' country in war time, which I do not admit, I would still say that it is a proper tax because it i6 more important that this money should be raised in war time than that even capital should come in. What about after the war? This tax is limited to three years. I am free to say that an excess profits tax is not a good tax in times of peace because I think then it would have the effect which my hon. friend suggests and that effect would not be good for the country. But this tax is limited by its terms to a three year period. If this war goes on-and I confess it looks to me as if it would go on-it might go on for another year, or even longer-then we would have to consider broadening the basis of our taxation. We might have to resort to other modes of taxation, some of which were suggested in this House when the Excess Profits War Tax Bill was under consideration last year, and which have been mentioned in the course of this debate. But it is not necessary to consider these now. We are taking one step at a time in our taxation, and I submit that it is sound. When the war broke out, it would have been a great mistake to have suddenly developed a formidable scheme of taxation. The effect would have been bad upon industry and upon the public.

Is .my hon. friend
aware that the financiers of the United States announced it as their purpose to make the men of the present day pay their full proportion of the cost of the war and not leave it to the boys after they come home from the front?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me point out the distinction between the case of the United States and Canada. We have been bearing the burden of this war for three years. In the case of the United States, one of the wealthiest countries in the world-
What about England?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will come to England in a moment-and one of the greatest, they enjoyed a period of prosperity for the past three years. When this war broke out, the immediate effect in Canada was a dislocation of the business of the country. To have imposed a heavy burden
of taxation at that time would have been unwise from every standpoint. The result was that when the war broke out we imposed a moderate measure of taxation and in the following session raised the tariff by 7\ and 5 per cent and imposed special taxation calculated to realize a substantial sum. Last year we imposed the excess profits tax and this year, as these profits have become greater, we have increased the excess profits tax. Our taxation from the beginning, has been, I submit, scientific, and has progressed in such a manner as not to unduly disturb the industries of the country, hut rather to promote business and not to discourage our people. To have imposed as heavy a burden of taxation as we have to-day upon the people at the outbreak of the war would have been disastrous from the business standpoint and would have discouraged the people.
Will not my hon. friend withdraw the word 'scientific"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will be prepared to argue that if my hon. friend desires. As to the excess profits tax, I would call his attention to the fact that we are in very good company.
How would one conceive of the methods of taxation adopted by the Government as being scientific?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The burden has fallen upon those who are best able to bear it.' We have not taxed those engaged in the basic industry of the country-agriculture; we have imposed no direct taxation upon the ordinary citizen or artisan. Whom have we taxed? We have taxed those who can afford to Tide in Pullman cars, like the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt).
What?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I say we have taxed those who can afford to ride in Pullman cars like the hon. member for North Oxford.
I always take the smoking car ahead.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has been found in a Pullman car, and I am quite sure he does not sleep in the smoking car. We have taxed banks, trust companies and loan companies; we have taxed them all; we have taxed excess profits; now we are taxing excess profits some more, and if that is not scientific all I have to say is that

it has 'been found to be a pretty good system of taxation. It has met with the approval of the people.
Mr. MeCEEA: You will find out what the people of the country think about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend says that we will find out what the people of the country think about it. I do not believe that my hon. friend, in these matters, is the spokesman for the people of this country. My hon. friend, I know, is annoyed about this measure. There is no question but that the industry in which he is interested will be hit by it, but there is no doubt, also, of the fact that the industry can stand it. Here is another point: it will not be hit by this measure unless it is doing well. Unless it is making profits it will not have to give any profits to this Government. That is the particular merit of this Bill. A man will pay only if he is making big money. If that is not a scientific measure of taxation I do not know what is.
The minister lias not answered the question that I put to him before he rose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to how much will be realized?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not yet
possible for me to give even an estimate.

You have the
statements given ,to the department by those who were taxed last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have the
statements given to the department by those who were taxed for the first accounting period, and by some who will be liable for the second period, but not all. So far as the third accounting period is concerned, we have very few of those reports in. The result is that I am unable to make an estimate. But this is to be po-fhted out that it was last year that the large profits were made. That is to say, of the first three years I think last year was probably the best. Therefore this new taxation measure will apply more particularly to the larger profits of the third accounting period, and so substantial sums should be realized from it. It is not possible to make even a rough estimate, as we have no figures to which to apply the 50 per cent and 75 per cent taken from the excess profits.

Could the minister not
furnish to the House a statement of the excess profits which have .been made by one industry as an example? Take the flour milling industries of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could give them if they were asked for. As I said last year, if a motion is adopted in the House for returns of the assessment of this business tax, the papers will be laid on the Table.

Would there be any
objection to producing statements showing the persons, firms and companies, and the amount paid by them for the first accounting period?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would consider that. I do not know whether we have that information. We received some very large cheques in payment of these taxes.

The millers and the
ministers are partners in boosting the high cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see how that is.

The greater the cost
of flour the greater the revenue received by the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The excess profit tax comes second in point of time. The excess profit must exist before I can take the tax.

The big milling companies publish their statements and the companies have a good idea of their profits. But there are hundreds, and I trust thousands, of small milling companies and millers all over Canada, and I think the public have a right to know how much they are contributing and how this tax has been levied. That information should be brought down, I think, without Parliament demanding it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was discussed last year in the House, and I then made the same, statement that I have made to-day.

The reason I suggested the milling industry is because the people are intensely interested in the increasing price of flour, and I think that before we pass this Bill we ought to have a statement from the minister of the excess profits of the milling industry last year. I think the public would like to have that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That matter can be raised at any time. I do not^ think it

need be discussed in connection with this resolution.

Would the minister say why he is going to take only so much taxation from the people of Canada to-day? In view of the tremendous obligations we are assuming, is he not simply putting off the evil day? If the country is prosperous to-day, why does he not provide for a system of taxation that will be scientific in its character and put the burden on the people to-day, and not leave everything until the boys come home again?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I said today will still apply, that at present we are not only paying our pensions and the increased interest on our national debt, which is very large, but we have been able to pay $60,000,000 of the principal of the war indebtedness.

The hon. member
for Northumberland made the point that my hon. friend had taken $65,000,000 but had applied only $60,000,000 towards paying the debt created by the war. Did the minister have $5,000,000 more?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, because if
he had he would have applied it. We pay our ordinary expenditure, our capital expenditure, and then whatever balance there is is applied in reduction of the war debt.

The point made was that the minister derived $65,000,000 out of extra taxation but that he applied only $60,000,000 to the war debt, using the other $5,000,000 for the extra expense of ruling the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is entirely inaccurate.
The hon. member gave the details.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But even supposing it was so, does my hon. friend say that we should default as to $5,000,000 of ordinary expenditure?
You should economize; you are not economizing at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not economizing? If we had applied that $5,000,000 to the ordinary expenditure, we would have been able to apply .only $5,000,000 in respect of $25,000,000 of increased interest and pensions due to the war because the increased interest and pensions are charged to our ordinary expenditures.

You should have
spent less last year; you are extravagant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We have devoted $60,000,000 to the payment of the principal of pur war expenditure. It seems to me that that is a sufficient answer to the hon. member for Pictou. If this war goes on, as I stated in the Budget, and if our expenditure increases, as it probably will increase with the increase: in our militia, necessitating additional taxation to raise more money, then $60,000,000 is a very substantial amount to have paid in time of war on the principal of our war expenditure. In 15 years, at the same rate of payment, $900,000,000 of indebtedness would be liquidated.
At six o'clock, the House resumed, and then took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: Bill No. 41, respecting The Grand Trunk Pacific Branch,Lines Company.-Mr. Currie :

speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed Committee of Ways and Means, Mr. Rainville in the Chair.

When the House rose at six o'clock the Minister of Finance had been replying to various comments that had been made with regard to this resolution. This afternoon, when I read what the Financial Times had to say with reference to certain companies that were deterred by reason of the resolution from investing in this company, I simply gave the statement made by the Financial Times for what it was worth. I do not know as to the correctness or incorrectness of that statement. I did say that I believed if this measure were enacted it would deter capital from coming into this country, if the tax were not more equitably distributed. I said that I did not see why every person who made over seven per cent profit in his business should not be subject to paying his proportion of the tax. I said that so far as I knew the companies which would be affected by the fifty per cent tax and the seventy-five per cent tax would have no objection to paying their proportion of the taxation provided that every one else paid his proportion under the seven per cent



Clause, or under any ocf the other clauses of the resolution. My hon. friend argued, of course, as he did before, that it would be inconvenient to collect the tax from a person or company whose capital is only $50,000, and that a capital of $50,000 at seven per cent would earn only $3,500. That is no reason why such persons or companies should not pay their fair proportion of the tax. Every one in this country is willing to 'bear his fair share of the burden of taxation necessary to bring this war to a successful conclusion.
My hon. friend said that the main thing after all was the winning of the war, and with that we all agree. He said that if, in order to win the war it were necessary to do without capital coming into this country, he would be in favour of doing without the capital. If he carries that argument to its logical conclusion, why have these taxes? Why raise any tax? What is capital for but for the Government to use in carrying on the war? If his argument were carried to its ultimate conclusion, we would carry on the war without any capital or without any revenue. Such a position is, of course, absurd. We cannot get too much capital into this country to promote our industries and resources. That statement held good before the war and it will hold good during the war and after the war. We need in this country population and capital tnoTe than anything else. My hon. friend says that this tax will be limited to three years. I am afraid that he is not in a position to prophesy how long this tax will be exacted, and I do not think the people will grumble at how long it will be exacted so long as the revenue derived therefrom is properly used in the carrying on of the war. No one that I know of is grumbling at having to pay this war tax; what people are grumbling at is being selected as the only ones to pay the tax. I made that statement last year and I make it again now. My hon. friend, when he said that if, in order to win the war it were necessary to go without capital coming into this country, he did not care whether capital came in or not, knew that he was simply talking to the grand stand. We all know it is absolutely necessary to have capital to carry on the war. When in my boyhood days I used to play lacrosse, the boy who was disliked by the other boys was the one who played to the grandstand, that is the boy who kept the ball to himself and would not pass it along to the others.
There was no team play.
Yes. I was surprised to see the Minister of Finance playing a good deal to the grandstand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Was my hon.
friend engaged in team play with the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Douglas) in his attitude towards this taxation measure?

I certainly was not; I
did not even hear that hon. Imember's speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Then there was
no team play on that side?

Not so far as I was concerned. I was speaking with reference to the interest of the country and without reference to party at all. What I objected to in the minister's grand stand play was this: he said that the men and women of this country who were sending their boys to the front were doing more than any one who was paying taxes in this country. I was discussing the financial end of the matter; I was not discussing the sentimental nor the moral end. My hon. friend is not the only one in this country who feels for the men and women who have sent their boys to the front. Many a man in this country who is paying excess profits taxes has sons who are fighting at the front, and some of whom have died at the front, and yet there is no grumble on their part. If what the minister said was not grand stand play, then I do not know what grand stand play is. I had no intention of mixing up the question of the men who have risked their lives with this financial discussion this afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I interrupt my hon. friend, because I should not like him to misunderstand me. I had not in mind to suggest that the hon. member was actuated by any such motive; but the article which he read to the House, it seemed to me, unduly emphasized the money aspect of this excess profits tax, and it was rather to that than to the remarks of my hon. friend that I was addressing myself. I entirely acquit my hon. friend of being actuated by any other motive than that of discussing this subject in this House in a business way.

I thank the minister, and I freely accept that explanation from him. So far as the article in the Financial Times is concerned, I am not accustomed to quoting newspaper articles, but I gave it for what it was worth. I did not say that these companies were deterred from

investing capital in this country, because I was not aware of anything of the kind. I would like to say one word with reference to income tax. My hon. friend complains that he cannot impose an income tax conveniently owing to the municipalities and the provinces also having the right to exact an income tax. I would suggest to him that the matter could be worked by excepting the amount paid to the municipalities and the amount paid to the provinces, that is to say, by giving the person who is paying under the Dominion tax credit for what he had already paid on account of the municipal and provincial taxes. I do not know that I have anything further to say in regard to the matter. I give my views honestly for what they are worth, without regard to party in any manner, shape or form.

I have a few observations to address to the committee before the adoption of the resolution. The consideration of a taxation resolution is a matter of business, and I quite agree with my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), that there is not much necessity for exhorting hon. gentlemen to unite for the winning of the war when a matter of this kind is under consideration. As to the winning of the war, we are all agreed. But the consideration of taxation proposals in committee, is ordinarily, a time when we come to close quarters in discussion, and when there is more or less frankness. The Minister of Finance referred this afternoon to the fact that some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House had approved of the taxation proposals now under consideration. That is quite true. The hon. member for South Cape Breton in discussing the Budget this afternoon openly and very emphatically approved of the taxation proposals. On a matter of this kind one would naturally look for differences of opinion. There should not be a tendency to discuss taxation proposals from a point of view altogether partisan. There is a differenue of opinion, for instance, among hon. gentlemen on this side of the House as to the desirability of the proposals of the Minister of Finance, and it is desirable to have hon. gentlemen express .their views, whether favourable or otherwise. On the other side of the House there are hon. gentlemen who will probably support the proposals of the Minister of Finance; at least, I can safely say they will not oppose them. Nevertheless, it does not follow that in their best judgment these proposals are altogether
92i
wise, and just, or necessarily in the interests of the country. It is more difficult perhaps for hon. gentlemen opposite to indulge in the same freedom of criticism as hon. gentlemen upon this side of the House. I think it is very important indeed that we should have the utmost freedom in discussing a matter of this kind. I do not pretend to insinuate that the Minister of Finance does not entertain that view.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I invite the
utmost freedom of discussion, because it will he of the greatest benefit to us.
iMr. A. K. MACLEAN:	Litigation in
court for instance is justified on the ground that from the conflict or shock of opposing views the court may reach the truth approximately. Similarly, through the conflict of opinion that may arise in this committee, the (Government may readh the best possible system of taxation fitting the circumstances.
There is another matter I wish to refer to, and my attention was directed to this by a reference of the Minister of Finance this afternoon to the fact that in several of our provinces there is already a certain form of income tax. It has often struck me that there should have been a conference between the Dominion and provincial governments in reference to taxation. During the last two or three years it seems to me that many of the provinces have practically exhausted every method of taxation within their powers. The province of Ontario, particularly, has initiated very wide taxation schemes; perhaps they were necessary, and perhaps they were not. But it is just possible that the province might have avoided such extended taxation by economies or reforms of some kind, and if so, it was their duty to have done so. I think it would have been desirable for the Minister of Finance to have met the provincial governments in conference a long time ago, and asked for their co-operation in the matter of financing the war. This would have given him an opportunity to present to them most clearly and forcibly the probable obligations that will rest upon the Federal Government in the future, and I think in that way he would have gained the co-operation of the provinces.
I would not undertake to say that the fresh taxation proposals of the Minister of Finance are altogether unpopular. They will be unpopular with the men who will have to pay; there is no doubt about that. But, after all, that applies to such a small

proportion of the .population of Canada that these proposals are bound to be very-popular with the great majority, who will not have to pay them. I suppose that if a man were viewing these proposals purely from the standpoint of political safety he would rather take the position that the proposals on the whole were pretty good, because the great majority of one's constituents shall not 'be affected by them. However, I do not consider that is a fair method of considering a matter of this kind, particularly on the part of public men who must assume the responsibilities attaching to they: position. We do know that persons and corporations liable to taxation under these proposals are protesting in large numbers and quite vigorously; perhaps it is true that in many cases their complaints are hardly justified, because the additional taxation to be imposed would mean very little beyond what they have to pay under the Act of last year. To some, however, it will Ibe quite a serious matter, and it is easy to understand there may well be an *honest difference of opinion as to whether or not it is desirable to increase the business profits tax, and obtain additional revenue from other sources.
The Minister of Finance justified all his taxation schemes this afternoon ion the ground of their being scientific. Of course, if they are scientific, they are absolutely sound. I suppose, however, the minister was using language rather loosely when he employed the term "scientific." He said that he started out by having recourse to one source at one time, and to another source at another time. But it might turn out that all these sources shall be exhausted or dried up when he turns to them later when his financial necessities are urgent. Our obligations this year are probably as heavy as they will be in any year in the future, no matter how long the war continues. The country is fairly prosperous. The average citizen is in rather happy circumstances to-day. Therefore, I say, this is the time to apply all possible forms of taxation, this is the best opportunity we shall have to secure for Canada the largest possible revenue in order to lessen the total of our public debt upon which the people will have to pay interest after the war. That there is an element of fairness in the business profits tax no one will deny. It may be true, also, that the Act of last year was on the whole a justifiable method of taxation and was perhaps quite popular in the country. The only objection I had to it-and I ex-

pressed myself so at the time-and the only protest I have heard from other citizens, is that it should be applied more widely. It was pointed out by hon. members on this side last year, and events have proven the soundness of their contention, that in some localities yon will find a firm or partnership earning, it may be, $50,000, and paying a substantial tax, while in the same place there may be another concern with earnings of $100,000, yet paying nothing. I think that inequalities of this kind irritate the community -and render that form of tax unpopular. It would- have been better, had the business profits tax had a wider application, not only because it would have been more in accordance with justice, but because the treasury would have benefited. The increased business profits tax will yield but little additional revenue; will impede industrial expansion, prevent the inflow of foreign capital. It would have been better to adopt- some other form of taxation. I am not, however, referring to concerns engaged in purely war supplies.
There is another aspect of the case which makes me think that you cannot infer the desirability of a business profits tax for Canada by showing that it applies well in England. In Canada there are very few businesses with enough capital. Many have sufficient invested capital, but the working capital, as a rule, is borrowed. Our business concerns are usually very heavy borrowers from the banks. In England, not only is there an abundance of invested capital, but the great industrial concerns there, as a rule, have large reserves. I read pretty regularly a financial journal published in London, The Statist, a journal which the Minister of Finance knows very well. Each issue gives the proceedings of annual meetings of important companies. In reading these reports, I notice that invariably they disclose a very substantial cash reserve accumulated in the course of years of operation of these concerns. Consequently, these concerns are not borrowers from the banks. On the conclusion of this war, there will 'be a period of anxiety for industrial concerns in this country. Many of them to-day carry contingent accounts, that is, they are setting aside a portion of their profits to meet contingent liabilities that may arise on the cessation of war. The cost of raw material may go up, or there may be many contributing causes to lessen profits. Therefore, they feel that a cash reserve is desirable against the time when a business depression will come and when

the banks may find themselves not in a liquid position to justify large loanings to industrial concerns.
My substantial objection to the resolution, is that which I voiced last year against the business profits tax, and that is that the efforts of the Government to secure revenue to meet our heavy obligations are too restricted. As I pointed out when speaking on the Budget, we are not paying enough of our annual war expenditure. It is eminently desirable that our national debt be kept down to the lowest figure possible, so that the country may be able, without distressing itself, to take care of its fixed charges and have sufficient revenues to carry on public services with efficiency. There are many people, I am sure, who would be quite happy to be compelled by law to pay something to the treasury who are not paying anything today. So, I say, the tax proposals contained in the resolution are too restricted, and also they are unjust to the small number who are obliged to pay. The result is that the treasury is not receiving the volume of revenue which could easily be had and which the country requires so much, and will require so much in the future. I put the case to the minister this afternoon that, if a man were in receipt of an income of $50,000 from invested capital, there was no reason why he should not be compelled to pay something toward the public revenues for war purposes. I can not conceive of any answer to that proposition. His income arises from capital which he has invested, and is more than he requires for his personal purposes. Most persons in that position would be willing to contribute a very substantial portion of that income to the treasury for war purposes.

Have these people, who are so anxious to pay taxes, ever heard of a Patriotic Fund, a Red Cross Fund, or any similar institution to which they are free to contribute and by which their money would be cheerfully accepted?

I have no doubt that that class of people do contribute very generously to the Patriotic Fund and other similar causes. And so they should. The Minister of Finance stated this afternoon that if a business concern earns over fifteen per cent, it should not complain if the country takes fifty per cent of its surplus earnings. But even if men of the class to
which I refer had contributed generously to the Patriotic Fund, that does not answer my contention that out of the very handsome surplus remaining above that which is actually required for their private purposes they should contribute a very substantial portion to the country for war purposes.
There is another point which I urged against the business profits tax last year, and which I still believe in. In England the business profit tax applies to profits earned over and above the average amount earned for the three years prior to the war.
I do not recollect at the moment what answer the Minister of Finance made to this point last year, but I remember that he did make some reference to it.' That always struck me as being a very fair provision, and there is a very strong feeling among business men of this country who are liable under the Business Profits Tax Act, that this same provision should be applied to companies and individuals liable under our Act. I think it is only a fair and just provision. The imposition of a tax upon profits earned above the average profits prior to the war is justly and truly a war business profits tax. The title of the Act at the present time is a misnomer, because it does not apply merely to profits earned by reason solely of the war, but it refers also to profits which would be earned in peace times. These, in a general way, are the observations which I wish to address to the committee at this time upon the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are a few more points which my hon. friend referred to, and which I desire to deal with briefly. But, before doing so, I should like to say that so far from deprecating criticism upon any measure which I have in this House, and especially a taxation measure, I invite it. I am pleased to say that I have derived, in connection with my measures in the House, a great deal of assistance from the criticism which has been offered. I would also like to believe that I am willing always to make concessions when it appears proper to do so, as the result of the criticism to which measures are subjected. Last year when this .business profits War Tax Bill was under consideration in this House, I received many valuable suggestions and the Bill was very much improved by them. As far as this amendment is concerned, I should like to have the frank opinion of every one in this committee and, if it appears that the Bill is too sevfere or that it is

going to work out disadvantageous^, having regard to the national interest, I am prepared to consider that criticism. But I rather did resent in connection with the bill-probably that is not the word, because I do not think a man should resent anything that occurs in the House of Commons-being criticised, on the one hand, because the bill was not nearly severe enough, and, on the other, because the Bill was so severe that it would injure capital, drive out capital, and prevent capital from coming in. That did not appear to me to be fair criticism from the Opposition benches, because the one attitude is entirely inconsistent with the other.
I gave the reasons pretty fully this afternoon why I thought it was inadvisable that we should resort to a federal income tax at this time. I do not propose to go over that ground again but under the existing law in most of the provinces in this Dominion, a man is fairly heavily taxed today upon his income (that is, if the law is administered), and if we imposed a federal income tax it seems to me it would he an additional impost upon him at this "time when the cost of living has greatly increased. There is another feature in connection with this that is put forward and that is, that companies are severely taxed by this excess profits tax. At the same time it is suggested that there should be also an income tax. I believe that if we imposed an income tax in addition to the excess profits tax it would fall to a large extent upon those who are already taxed by this excess profits tax. Take managers and [DOT]other officers of the companies that are taxed by this measure;, they derive their salaries, and those salaries are subject to taxation under income legislation in at least certain of the provinces in which they live. If we added on a federal income tax, we should be taxing these men upon their salaries notwithstanding the fact that many of these officers are interested in the companies which are taxed under this excess profits tax Act.
* There is another feature of it. Income is derived from personal earnings, or from interest on mortgages, bonds, and other securities and dividends upon stock. Insofar as income is derived from dividends on stock, the recipient of such income is already taxed by reason of the fact that he is a shareholder in these companies subject to the excess profits tax. That has to be borne in mind. What I stated this afternoon, and what I desire to repeat, is,

that we may come to the time "when we shall have to resort to income tax. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) said: why not do it now? The reason I think it inadvisable to do it now is that income? are already subject to taxation by municipalities or provinces, and it does not seem to me that the burden should be placed upon the average citizen deriving income which would be subject to taxation, until the necessity is absolutely clear and until it is indispensably necessary in the national interest that we should impose such taxation. Take the lawyers in Canada, and I only speak of them as one class who are subject to income tax by municipalities and provinces; I do not believe that the income of lawyers has been increased since the war broke out. I believe rather that the contrary is the case. I do not believe that the income of physicians has been increased and I do not believe that the incomes of most of those who derive salaries from their employment has been increased. That is on the average; I suppose some of them have been increased and others have been reduced. But, the cost of living has gone up. Is it indispensably necessary at this time to tax all those who may derive incomes throughout the country? You could hardly select nine or ten large incomes and make them a special object of taxation. You could not introduce a Bill for the taxation of half a dozen or a dozen or twenty men in this country. Your income tax would have to be general. I am only pointing out these aspects of the matter because it seems to me that they are relevant to the question as to whether an income tax should be imposed now. My view has been that it should not be imposed now. My hon. friend has said, and his words are true, that people have paid this business tax gladly. I bear cheerful testimony to that. The spirit in which the excess profit tax has been borne has been admirable. Men have not been anxious, so far as I am aware, to avoid taxation; they have been desirous of contributing, and have willingly paid the taxation against them. That taxation, in many cases, has run into very large sums of money. The hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is always a valuable contributor to a debate, and I certainly had not in mind, when I spoke this afternoon about the sacrifices the people of this country are making, anything that he himself had said. But there has been a criticism of this measure which I do not believe is just, in

that it emphasizes the large sums of money which will have to be paid into the federal exchequer. I do not believe that that is a sound criticism of the measure. It would be a sound criticism to say that it is not fair, if that is the view of the critic, that only those having a capital of $50,000 or more should be assessed. That is a criticism that may fairly be put forward, to be met by us who believe that the line has to be drawn somewhere, and that if it is not drawn at $50,000 it would have to be drawn at $40,000, for the reasons which I gave last year. But I do not believe that it is fair to say at this time that the measure is objectionable, and to severely criticise the Government on the sole ground that large sums of money are taken from the industries of this country; because in a time of sacrifice such as this, money becomes of entirely secondary importance. It is very important, but it is of secondary importance. It is needed and will be needed for the prosecution of the war, and I have been unable to see, and I am still unable to see, why, if firms or companies are making huge, even abnormal earnings, a very substantial portion of those earnings should' not be taken for the treasury of the state engaged in the prosecution of - this war. That is what I had in mind this afternoon when I referred to the sacrifices which are being made in this country, and I think it desirable from time to time to emphasize that feature, certainly not in censure or criticism of any member of this House, but only because we are taking extraordinary action on account of extraordinary conditions. I assure hon. members that it is no pleasure to me to incur the criticism which I undoubtedly do and will incur in connection with a measure of this kind, which does take a heavy toll from many of our industries. It is no pleasure to bring it down, and it is not brought down with any object of political aim or advantage, although I do believe that public opinion will support a measure that, at a time like this, takes a substantial part of large earnings made, and honestly made, for the purposes of the war.
The soundest criticism I have heard of this measure has been that it may take so large a sum from a firm or company that the company may not be able to raise that amount of money readily, and that it may, to a certain extent, make the position of the company unliquid. That is the soundest argument I have heard against thie measure, but I do not agree that the amount
taken, although large, is unduly large in war time.
My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), who, as usual, made a very temperate speech and put forward his ideas and criticisms very fairly, raised the question why we did not adopt the English policy of establishing the average earnings of a company for the three years preceding the war, and then take only a portion of that excess profit earned now over the average profit earned for those three years. We gave that matter a great deal of consideration, and I have discussed the English income tax with many who are subject to it.
I believe that our tax is a better tax, and . that is the opinion of many from the United Kingdom to whom I have spoken about it. What has happened in the United Kingdom is this:	Those companies' that did the
largest business before the war, that were earning 25 per cent, 30 per cent, or 40 per cent, are in many cases earning that amount to-day and yet are paying nothing. Their average, we will say, was 25 per cent or 30 per cent before the war. Since the war they may earn only the same amount, and yet they are going scot free. But companies that earned only 4 per cent or 5 per cent before the war, which perhaps had a run of hard luck, or were engaged in a business that was not thriving at that particular time, but are now making perhaps 40 per cent, find themselves mulcted to the extent of 80 per cent of their excess profits. In my opinion, it is very much better to fix a Tate of 7 per cent or 8 per cent or ten per cent as a standard for all companies, and then, if they make excess profits over that rate, to take a proportion of those excess profits. It must be borne in mind that we are not taking all these excess profits. We did not confine the companies to 7 per cent under the Business Profits Wax Tax Act of last year. We took only one-quarter of the amount earned over 7 per cent upon capital as defined in the Act. This year we take one-quarter over 7 per cent and up to 15 per cent. That is to say, if a company is earning 15 per cent, we leave it 13 per cent and we take 2 per cent. Then, between 15 per cent and* 20 per cent, we take one-half, that is 21 per cent. So that a company earning 20 per cent gives 41 per cent and keeps 151 per cent. Then we take 75 per cent over 20 per cent. That is a heavy tax, but we are here getting up to the point where the dividends are abnormal. Take the industrial companies listed on the stock exchanges of this coun-

try, and it is not very often that in peace time they show more than 15 to 20 per cent profit. I am aware that many commercial companies that are not listed do show very much larger earnings than that, but probably not when you take into account, what we do take into account in connection with this measure, namely accumulated profits and unimpaired reserve as part of their capital.
As I have said, I invite fair criticism of this measure. We do not want to unduly tax industry; we do not want to drive capital out of this country, and we do not want to prevent capital coming in. But I do feel that we have a duty towards the public, and that in connection with the prosecution of this war, if abnormal profits are being made in munition supplies or in anj^industry, which .on account of the war enjoys exceptional advantages and is making abnormal sums of money, it is our duty to take a substantial part of that money for the use of the State.
It may be that the Bill is too severe. I have always been willing, if that is shown to be the case, to make concessions, and I want to assure the House that instead of depreciating criticism I invite it.

If the hon. gentleman is so anxious for criticism possibly he will pardon me if I give him my view. I do feel like criticising the Finance Minister, not so much on account of the actual provisions of this measure as upon his general policy. I do not think that he is taking enough out of the people who are earning money and who are financially in fairly good condition. It is said that Canada is prosperous to-day. There is, no doubt, a considerable degree of prosperity among certain classes of people, though I am afraid that if the minister went into the ordinary labouring districts he would have a somewhat different story to tell. However, so far as the financial world is concerned, there is a great degree of prosperity. But my hon. friend must realize that that prosperity is the result of abnormal conditions and of the influx of an enormous amount of borrowed money that is being scattered all over the Dominion. I suppose my hon. friend, himself is spending $300,000,000 or $400,000,000 yearly in the Dominion which is absolutely borrowed money and upon which interest must be paid next year and the succeeding year and during the years of our children's children.- Then, another $300,000,000 or $400,000,000 are coming in from the Allied countries for the purchase

of munitions alone, and hundreds of millions are coming in for the purchase of natural products over and above what would be the legitimate price that we would ordinarily receive for those articles. This is making ia false prosperity which is not equally distributed among the different classes of people. It seems to me, therefore, that it is the duty of the Finance Minister to take -as much of this money as he can get his hands on, in order to avoid borrowing too much money and rolling up the public debt to too great an extent. I do think that in some cases he should make a distinction between the different classes of industries from which he is taking money by way of taxation. I do not think that my hon. friend is justified in taking the same percentage of profits from the regularly established companies that are carrying on the same business that they carried on before the war broke out -as he is taking from the mushroom companies which have been established as a result of the war, are making money out of the war and are doing nothing but a war business. There are hundreds of such companies in Canada. Hundreds of companies in Canada have never put a dollar of their own money into their business; or, if they did, they were allowed such prices that within the first five or six months of operation they got all the invested capital back again and are now making enormous profits upon invested capital furnished them by the Government. That class of industry should pay a much higher rate of taxation than the well-established Canadian industry which was in business before the war commenced and which hopes to be in business after the war is over. An instance of an industry which my hon. friend has taken by the throat and forced to sell its product at a certain price is that of the newsprint paper industry. Industries such as this which were here before the war and have been carrying on a legitimate business, are, no doubt making large profits and are contributing a large proportion of excess profits to the Government. But surely it is unreasonable to say that an industry of that kind should contribute the same proportion of its earnings or profits to the state as the munition maker, who never put a dollar into the business and who is taking out of it 40,50,60,100,300, and as high as 900 per cent-and this in a -case where you do not fix the price of the product.
Another criticism that I wish to make is one that has been reiterated in

the House a good many times. In fixing the minimum amount of capitalization in respect of which taxation shall be imposed, the minister has not, I think, gone far enough down in the scale. He says that one has to stop somewhere. I admit that, but instead of stopping at $50,000, I would go down to $25,000, and even lower. Every man must make some sort of sacrifice in order to furnish money with which we may take our part in winning the war. The sacrifice being made by the company that is losing 25 per cent of its excess profits over and above 7 per cent is a mere bagatelle com- pared with the sacrifices that are being made by the people who are contributing to patriotic purposes. Why should not a company capitalized at even $25,000, and making profits of 7, 8, or 10 per cent, be compelled to contribute its proportion of the war taxation? My hon. friend says that you ought not to tax the dividends on stocks because the company has already contributed a portion of its profits. That may be true, but if I have $1,000 coming in from one industry, $1,000 from another and similar amounts from others, and am getting a total of say, $10,000, why should I not contribute a portion of that amount to the State? The reason given by the minister is that the companies in which I have my money invested have already contributed a certain proportion of their excess profits to the State. I do not think that the argument is logical. I think that we should go down the scale as far as it is possible to go without involving too great a cost of collection. The minister will say that if too many small companies are included in the taxation, the cost of collection will be greater than the amount received, but I think you can go away below where the minister is to-day before you reach the point where the cost of collecting will exceed the receipts.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will recollect that there is no exemption of companies and firms engaged in the munitions business.

I am aware of that, but I have companies in mind which, with a capitalization under $50,000, are earning handsome dividends. This war has made it possible for hundreds

I think I may safely say thousands- of companies to get rich indirectly as the result of the war, though not engaged in manufacturing munitions. That is another criticism that I make in all sincerity. I could give the minister instances which have come within
my own personal knowledge, and I am satisfied that every hon. gentleman could give similar instances, of companies capitalized at less than $50,000, which are making big profits as a result of the war, but who are not contributing towards the war expenses. As to the question of incomes, it is not my
9 p.m. purpose to discuss that at length, because it has been discussed a good many times in the House. But there is hardly a city or a country district in Canada which does not contain a number of men who are in receipt of big incomes which go scot-free so far as taxation is concerned. I am sorry to say that a large proportion of those people do not even contribute to patriotic funds, Red Cross funds, or anything else of that nature, and I do submit that this class of people should be taxed. I make a more severe criticism of the minister for allowing these men to go free than I do of all the other things put together. I suppose there is not a man within the sound of my voice to-night who could not pick out half a dozen or a dozen persons in his own constituency who have accumulated a large amount of money, who never spend a five dollar bill unless they have to in order to .purchase the aotual necessities of life, and who salt their money away in bonds or stocks or stockings or banks-and contribute nothing in the way of taxation. The Legislature of New Brunswick a year ago imposed a direct tax in order to raise $500,000 for the Patriotic Fund; this method of raising the money was adopted in order to get after the men who would not contribute voluntarily. These people ought to be compelled to contribute a very large proportion of their incomes in order to assist in carrying on the war. The minister says that we *should not tax these people because they may be manager' of a corporation which is paying a large proportion of its excess profits. That has nothing to do with the matter at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I indicated that some of those who are receiving salaries from the companies were also shareholders in the companies. I agree if the manager is also a shareholder in the company-
That is worse. He enjoys a big salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A company is as I said subject to the tax, and the shareholder would also be liable to taxation upon income.

Why should he not be liable upon income? The most severe criticism I have to make to the minister in this whole business is the fact that when he issued his first call for an internal war loan -and he has repeated the offence in every war loan down to the present time-he persistently and deliberately provided, and advertised it to the world, that the man or woman who invested his or her money in that war loan would not be called upon to pay any tax which the Dominion might impose upon incomes. He has proclaimed this to the people of this country: You invest your money in this war loan and you will not have to pay an income tax. If the minister at any future time wishes to impose an income tax, he will have $350,000,000 of the savings of the people of this country exempt from taxation, and he has practically made it impossible to work out an income tax in this country in a fair and honest manner. I am not going to impute motives; I do not wish to impute motives to the minister or to any other man; but the result of his conduct and of his advertisements in the handling of these war loans is that he will meet witli a great deal of . difficulty in arriving at a fair and equitable income tax in Canada. There are cases of rich men investing a hundred thousand dollars, five hundred thousand dollars, a million dollars in these war loans, which are the greatest cinch that I know of in the financial world to-day. A man invests a million dollars of his wealth in war bonds, and when the income tax collector comes around to him and says: I want you to pay income tax, he replies: My money is invested in war 'bonds and I go scot-free. My hon. friend says it is open to argument whether or not we shall have an income tax and things are certainly looking serious; but he has spiked his guns before he comes to that position; he has put himself in a position where he cannot collect income tax on $350,000,000 of the savings of the people of this country, and I know no class of investors would be in a better position to pay taxes than those persons who have raised the $350^)00,000 of these internal war loans. My hon. friend may think my criticism is not as gentle as that of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), but it is just as sincere and it is given with just as good grace and with no more bitterness than has been that of my hon. friend from Halifax. I have presented these things as I view them; I trust the minister will take some notice of them, and I hope my views will  v
benefit him and, together with the criticism of the rest of my friends around me, the result will be that Canada will raise more *money to carry on this war as she goes along, and when money is plentiful, and that she will not borrow so much money now and have to pay more interest when the time of peace comes. I do not think I was ever charged with being a pessimist, but I do look with the very gravest apprehension upon the affairs of this country when peace comes. When I think of three or four hundred thousand soldiers returning to Canada-and I hope that number does return-and of three or four hundred thousand munition workers being practically thrown into the streets; when I think of the tremendous debt and of the enormous interest charge that must be met; when I think of the pensions that must be paid to our soldiers or their dependents'-a debt that must be met .even if we have to sell all our land and property to meet it-when I think of the falling revenues that will occur, I feel it is the duty of every man in this country, no matter whether he be a financial magnate or not, to try to see if we cannot keep this debt down to something like reasonable dimensions and collect as much money as possible out of the people to-day when they are well able to pay it. Every million dollars we take out of the people to-day in taxes means one million dollar less on which we shall all have t,o pay interest for all time to come.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend stated that he was more severe than our genial friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). He was a little more severe, but he was not quite as well informed. I do not think my hon. friend from Halifax will put forward the argument which my hon. friend (Mr. Carvel!) stated was his main one, in criticism of this measure, namely, that we had exempted the war bonds which we issued from any income tax imposed under the authority of this Parliament. I would agree with my hon. friend as to the extreme undesirability of issuing bonds subject to that condition, if it could be avoided, but I say to my hon. friend that I know this opinion will be confirmed by any financial man in this country or in the United States, namely, that we could not conceivably issue a loan to the people of this country and the . United States unless that provision exempting them from any income tax was inserted on the face of the loan.

My financial transactions * are, of course, very small compared with

those of my hon. friend, but I have a good many clients who invest money, iand I have never in my life had the question asked me by a client whether bonds were exempt from income tax or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be, but my hon. friend is thinking about peace time conditions, and I do not think the question would be asked under peace time conditions.
I am speaking about the war loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
What about internal
issues?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The same is true of them. You take those loans which we put out internally. The average citizen
probably does not stop to inquire, but his investments are only a fraction of the whole. It is the man who is accustomed to invest who considers his investments carefully, and it is the insurance companies, the loan companies and these other companies, which are most careful in regard 10 their investments.
It is an attraction, a necessary attraction in connection with war loans that they should be free of income tax. The issue that the United 'States is putting out to-day is free of income tax, tout not free, I believe, of succession duties. In England, the very home of income tax, in order to meet the situation in connection with their last loan they had to make a double issue, so to speak, one free of income tax and the other subject to income tax, with a very substantial difference in price .between the two issues. If we had put out our loan without the provision of exemption from income tax, we should never have been atole to sell it pn the same interest basis. Consequently it is as broad as it is long. What we might have realized hereafter by way of income tax legislation would have been lost at the time of the issue. I stated when presenting the Budget that if we had an income tax it would fail to reach a large proportion of pur population toy reason of that unavoidable provision in our bonds. I agree with my hon. friend that it is desirable to avoid such a provision if we possibly can, tout it could not have been avoided, and 1 submit that to the judgment of this House.
My hon. friend has raised the question of the paper industry, and I do not desire specially to discuss that matter to-night except to say this, and I do not know that these remarks will apply exclusively to the paper industry. It is of course a great industry whose development and success we are all interested in, but it would not be possible for me to look at it differently from any other industry. We have unlimited resources of the raw material which is the basis pf the paper industry, and it is a great industry to toe encouraged and developed. The situation in regard to the paper business was abnormal and exceptional. Why? Because of the limitation upon the supplies available at the present time The supplies of sulphite from Scandinavia are shut off toy the war, and the result is practically a monopoly in newsprint. I do not say that it is an intentional monopoly; I do not for one moment say that the men engaged in the manufacture of

newsprint are attempting to monopolize the situation, but a virtual monopoly does exist on this continent by reason of the limitation of the supplies, and the result is that the price of paper has gone up by leaps and bounds.
The cost of transportation too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was admitted in my office that the price could practically be fixed as was desired by the manufacturers, but they claimed that the prices which they were charging were reasonable. It is true that their costs have gone up. They had gone up last fall when the matter was drawn to my attention, and they have gone up, I believe, since. In order to deal thoroughly with the situation, the Government on my recommendation appointed a commissioner who is engaged to-day in investigating the cost of production and the conditions in connection with that industry. I might say here, that there is no question in this country or the United States that has given the governments of both countries more trouble than this difference of opinion existing 'between the press and the newsprint manufacturers. This matter has been adverted to so often in this debate that I take this opportunity of saying that in November last I was waited upon by representatives of the press of this entire country, all sections being represented from Halifax to Vancouver, Liberal and Conservative alike. They drew my attention to the fact that under the prices then existing-and they pointed out what was open to them in the way of increasing the price of their newspapers and the charge for advertisements-they were threatened with ruination. It was not difficult to figure; they used so much newsprint; the price had jumped from such a figure to such a figure, and there was the net result. In many cases the earnings were wiped out completely, and in others they were substantially affected. I did not go out for the purpose of inviting the press to ask me to take up this question; the press came to me as they came to the authorities in the United States, and asked that the question be taken up as it was vitally affecting their business. This was in November. I called a joint meeting and the matter was so urgent that I called it on a holiday, Thanksgiving Day. I asked the newsprint manufacturers and the newspaper publishers to send repre-

sentatives to Ottawa, and they came and we held a joint meeting. I said: " Gentlemen, I do not want to interfere in this matter at all; it is an invidious task interfering in matters of this kind; I realize how complex this situation is, and I want you to appoint a committee of three from each side and see if you cannot reach a basis that will be fair." I pointed out that the war had created an exceptional condition, that supplies were hardly available from Scandinavia, that the situation was such that a virtual monopoly existed, that the profits of the sulphite and paper companies appeared to be large-and I had figures in substantiation of that placed before me-that on the other hand the newspapers were very hard hit and some of them threatened with ruin. I pointed out that the press was not a private enterprise, that although privately owned it had a quasi-public character, and that I did not think any government in this country could stand by and -see the destruction of the press on any substantial scale, and I stated that representative newspaper men in this country had represented that unless .something were done that would be the inevitable effect of the increase in prices. The committee that was appointed failed to reach a working basis.. They continued their negotiations, I believe, during my absence in England in November, and on my return the matter was again brought to my attention by the press. It had become still more urgent, and finally, having regard to the public interest and the desirability, as I conceived it, that the press of this country should be continued and not be ruined, we looked into the matter further and an Order in Council was passed which gave us power to deal with the situation. I differentiate that case absolutely from an ordinary business, because as I have said the press is quasi-public in character, especially in war time, and also because of the exceptional circumstances surrounding the paper industry by reason of which supplies ordinarily available in peace time were not available then, and the price had risen to a figure very much in excess of what at that time, at all events, appeared to be justified by the increased cost of production. We were not alone in that action, though we	dealt	with	theCanadian situation	only. At	thesame time the situation was	beingdealt with	on	the American	side,
and there certain prosecutions were instituted. I pass no opinion upon these, as I do not know the facts. But what I say

is that an extraordinary situation existed in the United States and in this country, so extraordinary that the Government there is concerned about it and action has been taken there looking to the relief of the press, and action was taken on this side, having a similar object in view. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell) asks why the paper industry should not be put in the same category as the manufacturers of munitions. We are not discriminating against any industry by this taxation, for practically all industries in Canada are subject to it. But the paper industry has enjoyed exceptional profits by reason of the limitation upon the usual supplies of sulphite on this continent. I do not know what the situation is to-day, we are investigating it. But I know that the profits made in some eases have been exceptionally, abnormally, large.

Have these exceptional
profits been made from the manufacture of newsprint or from other branches of the industry?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say as to that. The businesses are different. It was brought to my attention when I had this matter under consideration that some newsprint manufacturers produce their own sulphite-, while others buy their sulphite from the manufacturer of that product. Some sell exclusively in the United States, some exclusively in Canada, and some find markets in both countries. The investigation of the newsprint business would inevitably involve an investigation of the sulphite industry. I dealt with an association, the Pulp and Paper Association, and, certainly, precipitate action was not taken. It was only when all the resources of persuasion had been exhausted that we took the action we did. I believed that they had the power, by adjustments among themselves, to bring it about that reasonable prices could be granted to publishers of Canadian newspapers. I felt more justified in taking the attitude I did because they had the American market- and the Canadian market is only about tne-sixth of the entire market. They could afford to deal reasonably, very reasonably, with these customers here, who are hard hit by the war, and who have been their customers for many years. The action we took, I think, was absolutely justified as a war measure. I believe that if we had not taken it the effect upon the press of this country would have been most serious- I use no stronger term.

I assure the Minister of Finance that I would not set my knowledge of finance against his, or that of my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). Yet, notwithstanding his very laboured explanation, I am not satisfied. It is very easy for him to advance theories which he has never worked out in practice, and to argue from these theories. But I would like to have seen him try to raise an internal load without attaching to it the statement that it would not be liable to income taxes. According to his ideas of finance, this would not do. But he has not tried it out. In view of what he has said, what becomes of all the newspaper articles we have seen for the last year about the patriotism of our financial people in raising victory loans? If what the hon. minister says is correct, these people were making a shrewd business bargain, and if they had seen a fifth, of a point, or even a tenth of a point, of advantage in placing their money elsewhere, they would have placed it elsewhere. I do not believe that.; I believe the financial people of Canada have more patriotism than he gives them credit for, and that they would have invested in the war loan, even if he had not put in that rider about income taxes. I think he should have taken the chance, even if he had had to sell the bonds at a little less than he received for them. The revenues he might have received by taxes on the income of these bonds would have been much greater than the small discount he might have had to allow in selling the bonds. As I say, I do not put my knowledge of finance against his, but I am simply putting forward the views of a man from the country who has given some thought to these matters.
As to the paper business, I had no object in referring to what the minister did in relation to this business, except to compare with the way in which he has treated these concerns whose profits are regulated by the open market and the way he has treated his friends, the munition manufacturers, some of whom have made nine hundred per cent profit. I do not know, nor care, very much about the manner in which the price of newsprint paper is fixed. But if it was such an easy matter, and involved so little harm, to take these people by the throat and say, "You should not charge more than so much for paper," why could he not have applied the same doctrine to the people who are selling wheat at $3.25 a bushel and making millions and

hundreds of millions out of it to-day? Why could not he apply these measures to the dealers in many other products that are being sold at fabulous prices? This is not germane to the subject under discussion, yet I could not help reminding my hon. friend of some of the powers conferred upon the Government by the War Measures Act. We have discussed this before, and I suppose we should have nothing more to say about it now. But, if the minister be in a receptive mood, I hope that before these resolutions are acted upon, he will give these matters serious consideration and see if he cannot in some way get more money out of the moneyed people during the times of present prosperity. He should invoke - some new measure of taxation, and make the man who has a large income contribute a portion of that income to the state and put our finances in a better position than, I am afraid, they are in at the present time.

Criticism has been levelled at this excess profits tax ever since it was enacted.
