The two main criticisms that I have heard during the past year have been dealt with to a certain extent by my hon. friend from Car-leton (Mr. Carvell). One of these criticisms is that the hon. the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) has made no distinction whatever between the ordinary, regular business concern that had been in business for five, ten or perhaps fifty years previous to the war, and which was doing a fair and legitimate business, and those companies that have been established for the purpose of supplying war munitions to the Government. In many cases, especially in connection with these larger companies, the Government has supplied all the capital for these, enterprises. They granted them contracts running into the hundreds of thousands, millions and tens of millions of dollars for the manufacture of shells and-I am not complaining of it- they gave them prices on the first orders, three, four and five times the amount that it cost to manufacture the shells, for the express purpose of enabling these companies to pay for their plants and buildings and to give them a handsome profit the first year. Granted that that was all right, on what ground and justification does my hon. friend put that company on the same level as the legitimate business enterprise that may have been struggling for ten, fifteen or twenty years and which, when times became good owing to the war, has made a profit, although it had not been making

one dollar of profit for three, four or five years previous to the war? Why, I ask, does the minister put a legitimate business enterprise of that kind on the same footing as a war munitions profiteer? That is the criticism that has been heard all over the country. I do not believe that the men who are paying these war taxes to-day are complaining because they have to pay them, but their ground of complaint is that only one man with money in ten is being taxed at all. It is not the amount of taxation that is being taken out of the manufacturer that is causing him to complain. The main ground of complaint is that he is singled out and all the moneyed people are allowed to go scot free.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who are singled out?

I say that the manufacturers and business men of the' country paying this excess war tax .are not complaining about what they have to pay, but what they are complaining about is that they are . singled out and called upon to pay it while nine others who are making an equal or a greater amount of money are not even asked by the Government to pay one dollar.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Who has my hon. friend in mind when he speaks about men who are making an equal or greater amount of money than the munition or other manufacturers?

Let me give my hon. friend an instance. There are in the city of Ottawa, and in every city in the Dominion, men walking around the streets who are making from $100,000 to $200,000 clear cash every year out of their investments, and they are not called upon to pay one dollar. My hon. friend knows it perfectly well. That is not fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If they are in business-
But they are not in business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, then, we
must have an income tax to reach them. You could not single them out by a special Act. Are they not subject to income tax in Ontario? For instance, they have an income tax in Ottawa ; are they not subject to it?
There is no income tax in Ontario for war purposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not mean for war purposes.

My hon. friend is raising this tax for war purposes and he singles out one roan in ten and imposes this heavy tax on him, while the other'nine men who are making money much more easily, who are not employing anybody and who have incomes ranging from $5,000 up to $200,000 escape. My hon. friend says to them: we do not ask you to pay a dollar. That is what the men who are paying this tax complain of. They do not complain of the amount they are called upon to pay, but they do complain because they are singled out. One-tenth of the population has to pay $12,500,000, and all the millionaires and multi-millionaires are allowed to go scot free and are not asked to pay one cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Are not the incomes of most of these men derived from dividends on shares in companies which are subject to this tax? I believe they are.

Supposing they are, is that any answer to the argument? Take, for instance, the case of a man who has money invested in bank stocks. The banks do not pay any tax under this Act, but they pay a tax under the Act that was put in force previously, the Act imposing taxation on loan companies, insurance companies and banks. Supposing that a man has money invested in bank stocks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Banks are liable to. this tax if they make sufficient profits.

The tax is so fixed that it does not reach the banks as it reaches the manufacturers, except such as the little bank in my constituency which has a paid up capital of $250,000. The banks pay the tax that my hon. friend put upon them a year ago. But take the case of a man who has 100 or 1,000 shares in the Bank of Montreal. The Bank of Montreal pays whatever tax my hon. friend has put upon it and it is a very mild tax, but does the paying of that tax keep the bank from paying the dividends that give the man who is walking around the streets of Ottawa an income of $50,000 or $100,000? Because that man gets that dividend from the banks which pay this small tax is that any reason why the man receiving probably $100,000 a year should not pay anything? It is the most absurd thing that I ever heard of. This excess business tax is a tax made for the one and single purpose of letting nine millionaires or rich men out of ten escape altogether without even being asked to pay the tax. That is what my hon. friend from
Sherbrooke (Mr. McCrea) objected to, not to the tax that he had to pay. I do not think I heard one word of objection from my hon. friend to paying the amount he had to pay provided there was an even tax all round and that other men who had an income equal to his should pay their share.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is contending really for an income tax? Is that not really it?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh.
My hon. friend can call it what he likes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is my hon. friend then in favour of an income tax?

Certainly; I think it is absurd that a man who is working hard in business, employing hundreds or thousands of men and women, helping the development of the*country and who makes, say, $50,000 a year should be discriminated against. The manufacturer who makes $50,000 a year should undoubtedly pay heavily out ,of it in taxes, but why should the man who has $1,000,000 invested in bank and railway stocks and bonds that pay 5 per cent, who is doing nothing except cutting off and cashing coupons, but who makes $50,000 a year cash income, pay not a dollar towards the cost of prosecuting the war? Why should the one man pay $10,000 or $15,000 in taxes and the other pay nothing? If my hon. friend is trying to avoid taxing this class simply because he sees that it will be difficult to collect the income tax, that is simply begging the question. As has been pointed .out by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Carvell), the Minister of Finance has so placed his loans in Canada that when another $500,000,000 that is now lying in the banks drawing 3 per cent is put into Canadian bonds for the carrying ,on of this war, and we have altogether one thousand millions of Canada s savings invested in war loans, none of it paying one cent of income tax, guaranteed by the terms of the bonds against the imposition of such a tax, then my hon. friend in two or three years, if he is still in power, will come forward and say: Well, the time has come when we ought to have the income tax, but unfortunately there is one thousand million dollars of the investments of Canada on which we cannot collect an income tax. My hon. friend from Carleton never said a truer w.ord than that

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not quite so bad as that.

Well, if it is not quite so bad as that, my hon. friend must have it in his mind that it is pretty bad anyway. This discrimination is undoubtedly a source of dissatisfaction. I have never yet heard one man in Canada object to paying the tax; but I have heard hundreds object to paying the tax and having others get off scot free. I think my hon. friend should take into consideration a change in his system of selling bonds, in making future loans. Let him leave these bonds subject to income tax. The time is coming and is not far distant when we shall have difficulty in raising the revenue necessary to pay the pension fund, the interest on the war debt, the sinking funds, and all the expenses of running the country. I have noticed during the last day or two, in the disoussion of this measure, that my hon. friend lays- great stress on the necessity of winning the war. We all agree that we must win the war, and my hon. friend, of course, wants to keep the financial matters of the country right. Let me ask the minister if when, last year, he gave his authority and sanction to the handing over of $8,000,000 to Sir Rodolphe Forget for his railway, which he knew then and knows now will never, as long as my hon. friend or the youngest hoy in this House survives, earn one cent of interest on the money-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Is my hon.
friend not talking about the National Transcontinental Railway?

I am talking about the $8,000,000 which my hon. friend gave to his political associates, and I am asking him if he thought that he was helping to win the war by giving that $8,000,000 to Sir Rodolphe Forget. There is no man in this country- because I have a great respect for my hon. friend's ability

	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I doubt that sometimes.

I have a great respect
for his ability; but I should like to see him a little more free from the influence of some of his associates. My hon. friend would never have given that money of his own free will, I know him better than that. All I wanted to ask him was, did he think then and does he think to-day, that in giving that $8,000,000-'because it will cost Canada that much anyway, he was helping to win the war? That is a question my hon. friend has to consider.	.
Now let us see how much we are doing to pay for this war. This war has been going on practically within two or three months of three years, and during that time we have put $10,000,000, in round figures into winning the war-$10,000,000 of revenue, with all the taxation that has been put on the people. Do not let my hon. friend forget that at the first war session, the short session of five days, in August, 1914, he put on new taxes to the extent of many millions of dollars. Do not let my hon. friend forget that in the following session we amended the Customs Act again and imposed taxes of many million dollars on the people. Do not let him forget that, in addition to his custom taxes, he taxed everybody, poor and rich alike, by means of the stamp taxes and the railway ticket tax. * My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is accused of travelling in pullman cars. No doubt he does sometimes, but each time he pays his five cent tax on his ticket.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was only a joke.
(But the man who has to buy a railway ticket, the labouring man who buys his ticket from here to Aylmer, ten miles, pays the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He does not pay a cent.
Well he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Only when the ticket costs over a dollar.

Well, if he goes thirty-three miles he pays the same as the wealthy man who starts from here and goes to Vancouver and back. He pays practically the same amount. That is a tax on the poor man and as usual, the rich man is favoured. But with all those taxes that have been put on, the direct taxes and the custome taxes, my hon. friend has put only

$10,000,000 to the good towards the war in three years. That is the position Canada is in to-day. It is all very well to boast about what Canada i? doing, but I agree absolutely and entirely with the statements that have been made here this evening, that during this time, when we are getting in $1,000,000 a day for munitions of war, when orders to the extent of $1,500,000,000, practically, have been placed in Canada, on which probably $500,000,000 of money has been made in profits, out of those huge profits made last year and the year before, we have got in taxes from the wealth of Canada the paltry sum of $12,500,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How much does my hon. friend say has been spent on munitions? Did he say $1,500,000? If my hon. friend will go to the Munitions Board, he will find that it is not much more than one-third of that amount.

under which Canada secured her revenue. I quote from, a press report :
The contrast between the above revenue statement and the revenue statement of Canada: for the same period is startling.
Canada's total revenue for the fiscal year just ended amounted to the sum of $228,217,-2T0, the percentage of increase over that for the preceding year being almost equal to that of the United Kingdom. But what a difference there is in the sources from which it was obtained.
In Canada the customs tariff accounted for $133,531,155, or 58.33 per cent of the total revenue secured.
Excise accounted for $24,253,632, or 10.52 per cent of the total revenue secured.
Railways and canals accounted for $25,018,997, or 10.96 per cent of the total revenue secured.
Post office accounted for $20,031,627, or 8.77 per cent of the total revenue secured.
The masses contributed the greatest proportion of the above amounts. But out of the total revenue of $2i2S,217,270, excess war profits contributed the insignificant and paltry sum of $14,552,383, or only 6.58 per cent of the total revenue raised'.
In Britain excess profits and accumulated wealth contributed 60.23 per cent of the total revenue. In Canada excess profits contributed 6.58 per cent
It will be seen, therefore, that Britain gets the great proportion of her revenue from her wealth, whereas in Canada the great proportion of the revenue is taken from the poor people, and the wealthy go free. The system of my hon. friend taxes the poor and lets the rich escape. And, because my hon. friend is taxing only a few of the wealthy people of Canada, under the proposed provision that we are now considering, the rich will continue to escape taxation.
I hardly think my hon. friend is quite fair in this proposed legislation. I do not want to do my hon. friend any injustice. When he brought down last year the legislation that he is now amending he said that the legislation would be operative during a period of three years. Any one reading his speech would come to the absolute conclusion that that was a fixture for three years. My hon. friend now goes back on what we understood him to mean last year and is now putting an extra burden of taxation on the same shoulders on which he put it last year, after stating, as every one thought, that that was the end of that system of taxation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What I did say was that the Bill would last just the three years. I do not believe I said that the measure would not in any way be changed.

My hon. friend did not say in specific words: I will not come back

and augment those taxes. I will acknowledge that, but the general tenor of his remarks was that the tax was a fixture to the end of the three years, and no one looked for any changes along that line. Let me quote just a few of the remarks made by my hon. friend. While he was speaking on the 16th of March, 1916, he said:-
This is a temporary measure, and the operative part of it comes to an end at the date mentioned in the Bill, that is to say, the 31st day of December, 1917. It is true that in the succeeding year there will be a payment in respect of the accounting period falling due during the year 1917, but the Bill is designed to last only three years, and it will not last longer than that-

Did not my hen. friend,
when he was introducing this Bill, say that we might expect some further taxation later on?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I did not. Further taxation is possible, but I do not consider it necessary now to make any announcement along that line.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the matter with that? I say that further taxation is possible.

Later on in the same address, my hon. friend said this:-
This tax is, as I stated last night, for a limited period. My hon. friend questions whether I was justified' in making that statement. I certainly was justified in making that statement, because it represents the intentions of the Government. .	. That statement is in
no way inconsistent with that which I made iast evening, namely, that this particular measure is for a period only. The principle of the resolutions, it would appear to me, indicates that. .	. Therefore, it would seem to me
that I am perfectly justified in stating, as I do, on behalf of the Government, that this is a temporary tax. In making that statement, I largely meet the argument of my hon. friend that capital might be discouraged from embarking upon Canadian enterprise.
My hon. friend gave as a reason why capital would not be afraid to invest in Canadian enterprises, that he had fixed the rate and that it was only a temporary rate. Now my hon. friend comes back over the same ground and loads up the same people after they have invested capital, and says: Instead of taking 25 per cent, if you make big profits, we will take 50 or 75 per cent. While my hon. friend did not specifically say that he would not do this, he let the people believe and let capital believe that he would not do so, and no one could come to any other conclusion than that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In what my hon. friend has read did I not say it was possible there would be further taxation?

Yes, my hon. friend said it was possible there would be further taxa-

tion, and no doubt he was speaking then as he is speaking to-night to the effect that it might be advisable or necessary to impose an income tax. But there was nothing in the speech of my hon. friend last year that would, for one moment, lead any one to any other conclusion than that the tax he was then imposing on certain industries was a final and definite tax for three years, and that it would not ibe raised before the end of that time. That is the only conclusion that any man reading that speech could come to.
And that capital need not be scared because the tax was going to be only 25 per cent.

Later on in his Temarks, -my hon. friend said:-
This measure, therefore, being a temporary measure, it is not conceivable to me, when it is understood, that it will have any effect in retarding the flow of capital towards this country.
If, when my hon. friend made this statement, he had said:	Well this tax is for
three years; I am putting it on now, but possibly next year I may have to come forward and say that I am going to raise that tax of 25 per cent on profits ovier 7 pet cent to 50 per cent or 75 per cent, does my hon. friend for a moment thinik that would not deter capital from being invested? No man in Canada or elsewhere, after reading the report of the debate and the answers of my hon. friend could have come to any other conclusion than that, at all events for three years, there would be nothing more levied than 25 per cent on profits in excess of 7 per cent. It seems to me that my hon. friend is not doing himself justice on this occasion. I quite agree with him that more money must be levied. I would support him if he levied a tax that would enable us to collect $200,000,000 every year over and above the cost of running the country and if he put it into the carrying on of the war. He could get an extra $200,000,000 a year if he taxed every man of wealth in the same way as he is taxing men of wealth who have money invested in business or manufactures.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Do not you believe it.

That is what my hon.
friend ought to do. Let him bring forward an income tax. Let him tax every one alike; let him take not- only the extravagant amount that he allows his colleagues to spend but the pensions fund and the sink-
93*
ing fund and so on, but an extra $200,000,000 out of the people as the war is going on, and there will toe very little objection if it is done, not as my hon. friend is doing it now, tout in a fair, even way, so that the man who has $100,000 a year will pay more pro Tata than the man who has $5,000. .Let the minister do that and he will have all the income he needs and he will keep the finances of Canada in good shape; and let him also, when he makes further loans, eliminate that clause, that the bonds will not be subject to income tax, eo that when we come to levy an income tax-and there will be an income tax in Canada in a few years no matter which party is in power- we shall be in a position to say that every dollar of money invested in Canada shall pay its fair share towards paying the debt: of the war in adit'ion to the cost of carrying on the affairs of the country.
Mr. MeCREA: The Minister of Finance said this afternoon that last week I had been guilty of making a violent attack upon the Government, and especially upon himself. I wish to say that it was not my intention to be impolite or unreasonable in criticising the minister, although I criticised his method of taxation. I have no desire to be impolite or to use towards the minister or the other members of the Government language other than to criticise justly what I consider is entitled to criticism. The minister also stated that my criticisms were opposed to the tax.
If he will read my speech he will see that my criticism was of the inequality of the taxation; I said it was a tax bearing directly on but about five per cent of the population of Canada. If it were necessary, I said, I would be willing to be taxed 25, 50, 75 per cent, or even all my profits, provided everybody contributed in the same proportion; that was my attitude then, and it is my attitude now. I am still of the opinion that it is unfair and not in the best interests of the country to single out any one class and make it bear the whole burden. I have seen some criticism in the papers, and also heard some in the House, to the effect that, as I was a manufacturer, my complaint was purely an interested one. I do not suppose I could convince this House that such is not the case. Nevertheless, I wish to Bay that I have a very great interest in the welfare of this country. I have spent my life in doing a great deal of hard work, building up an industry with which I am still connected. But before my personal interests, I place the interests of my oountry. I believe the

effect of this taxation will have the effect of keeping capital out of this country, and I could not use a better argument than the one the Minister of Finance used a few moments ago when he told the House that it was absolutely necessary in floating the loans recently to specify in the prospectus that they would be free from taxation. Otherwise, he said, it would have been impossible for him to get anything like the same price for the issue. Well, if that applies to the selling of Government bonds, does it not also apply to the securing of capital for the development of this country? Comparisons have been made with the system of taxation in England. In my humble judgment, there is no comparison between this country and England so far as capital is concerned. This is an immense country, of untold wealth still undeveloped, and what we need for its development is, first, population, and secondly, capital, and if the Government by legislation frighten away capital, they will certainly not be helping to build up the country.
I said a moment ago that not over 5 per cent of our population would be directly affected by this taxation. But, indirectly, .it will affect everybody, because if capital is driven away from the country out industries will become dormant or die from lack *of capital, and then everybody suffers. I think it would be wise even at this stage for the minister to reconsider his measure o,f taxation with the object of devising some scheme for distributing the burden of taxation more evenly between all classes.
In his remarks this afternoon the Finance Minister stated that the first consideration was to win the war; he laid great stress on that. I hope that is what he had in mind when he was preparing this taxation. I hope I am wrong, but I fear he must have had in his head some thought of winning an election as well as winning the war. The minister said himself that this taxation was very popular. The reason it is so popular is because it is so unjust.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say it was popular. I said that I thought public opinion would sustain the measure. I did not use the word popular, so far as I recollect.

The minister said this afternoon that the people did not like taxation. Consequently, he exempts 95 per cent of 'the people from the tax, and puts the whole burden on the other 5 per cent. This will please the people, and will probably

be remembered when the proper time comes.
1	would like to say a few words about the paper business. I think in no other industry in Canada has so much energy been displayed and so much progress been made as in the production of paper of all kinds. To illustrate my meaning, I shall have to go hack in history a little. Some thirty-three years ago I supplied the fuel and paper wood for the Canada Paper Company, and I remember in the spring when I was receiving my cheque Mr. Thomas Logan, the president, said to me almost with tears in his eyes, "I do not know what is to become of this business. I am paying 50 cents a cord more for wood now than I ever did in my life before, and I am selling my paper for T| cents per pound less than a year ago." I knew what price he was paying for his wood, and I was curious to know the price he was selling his paper at, so I asked him, and he told me that the year previous the average price was 10 cents a pound, but that he could only get 8i cents at that time, and he almost had tears in his eyes at the thought of going into bankruptcy. To-day, before the war came on, newsprint was selling at about
2	cents a pound, and wood cost at least three times the price Mr. Logan had to pay then; that is, we were paying three times the price he was paying for his wood, and twice as much for labour and material, and yet the paper was selling for less than one-quarter the price he got thirty-three years ago. Yet he thought he would go into bankruptcy. I think this little story shows the great development that has taken place in the paper industry in this country, when newsprint can be produced so much cheaper than a few years ago. Down at Berlin in New Hampshire you will find a very large building in which are twenty or twenty-five men experimenting. If a man in the employ of a paper mill strikes an idea that seems to him an improvement in the processes or equipment of the works, he explains it to the manager. If the manager thinks there is anything in it he sends the man down to the building where the experimenting is going on. There the man finds draughtsman and all necessary assistance to put his ideas on paper. If the idea works out, well and good; his improvement or invention is adopted, and the inventor is rewarded. These are the methods employed by the paper manufacturers throughout the country, to produce paper at cheaper prices. The publisher wants all the benefit of this,

he wants to get paper at less than cost. Let me tell you the conditions in the paper trade prior to the war. You would think that when a man had cut his timber, driven it, and carried it through all processes of manufacture trO the finished paper and delivered that paper f.o.b. cars at the station, he had completed his part, and that the publisher to whom the paper was sold should pay freight and handle the product at destination. But that was not the case. The manufacturer had to prepay freight, and even prepay customs, and deliver the paper at Philadelphia or elsewhere, store it, and pay storage, and then deliver it to the publisher at the sidewalk each day for his next day's requirements. Now, nothing but keen competition would have driven men to such a position as that. The war came on, and everything in connection with the manufacture of paper went up in price. Pourdrinier wires, one of the big items, went up eight hundred per cent taking into consideration both cost and the life of the material. Is there any reason why the publisher, instead of crying baby and telling the Minister of Finance his tale of woe, should not have passed on his increased price as men in other lines of business have done? There was no reason why he should not have done it. Does any man believe that because you have to pay two cents for a paper that you used to buy for one cent you are going to stop reading the paper? Or that because you have to pay fifty per cent more for advertising space, you are going to stop advertising? That might be so if everything were dull and dead. Two years ago the clerks were standing behind the counters with folded arms and nothing to do. But to-day, business is good. I am n.ot referring to such conditions as those in Vancouver-you people there were in the land speculation business
I was smiling, but it was to see the leader on that side (Mr. Graham), who is a publisher, and is suffering under the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Mc-Crea's) remarks.
Not badly.
The Minister of Finance says that he has had more trouble over this than over all the rest put together.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No doubt about it.

I sympathize with the hon. minister, but the difficulty has not been caused by the manufacturers. They
have not been trying to get unreasonable prices. Whatever may have been done in other branches of the paper business, the demands in regard to newsprint have been very moderate.
What is the price of newsprint now compared with what it was before the war?
It was two cents a pound before the war, and now it is two and a half cents-an increase of twenty-five per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the actual price to publishers in the United States to-day?

It was three cents to
three and a half cents, and in some places more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman mentions a price of two and a half cents. That is the price existing as the result of the Government's intervention-But what would the price have been had it not been for the Government's action?

I think the minister himself gave the proper answer when dealing with the other branches of the paper business-that supply and demand should govern. That is what should have governed in the newsprint business as in everything else. And it would have been wisdom on the part of the publishers to have paid a little more for paper for the time being. There was a movement to start new industries in paper manufacture 'by men -who were imbued with the idea that there was all kinds of mpney in the business. They were looking out for new locations. But the moment the minister fixed the price of paper, he put the idea of big profits out of their heads, and they have gone home with their capital, and will stay there for some time. The publishers made the mistake of their lives when they undertook, through the influence of the minister, to fix the price oi newsprint at a cent a pound less than the article could be made for legitimately. No man can go into the business to-day and make paper for less than one cent a pound more than the price that has been fixed. The minister may say that, taking a mill that is equipped, to manufacture from the standing tree to the finished product, there is a margin of profit. But the average price of sulphite pulp is not less than $100 a ton,, and it requires 500 pounds of sulphite for one toil of newsprint. That represents $25-

for your sulphite alone. Then it takes 1,600 pounds of ground wood pulp, which is selling-and quick sale, as fast as you can make it-at not less than $40 a ton. That is, for 1,600 pounds, the cost would be $32. Add this to the cost of your sulphite and you have $57 for this material alone. Then take the high price of coal, the high price of labour, and other necessary expenses, and the total will run to $70 a ton before you touch profits at all, or three and one-half cents a pound.

This is a matter I know *very little about, but with the hon. gentle-unan's permission I would like to ask a question in order that I may learn something about it. Am I correct in saying that the output of newsprint in Canada is about 1,800 tons a day?
It is somewhere around that.

And the price before the war was two cents a pound, and now it is two and a half cents a pound? Assuming a year of 300 days, that would make a profit at present prices, over and above what they were before the war, of $5,500,000 a year, would it not? I presume they were not selling at a loss when they sold at two cents a pound?
They were not making any money.
There is this difference of $5,500,000-
What about the raw material?

That was the point I was coming to. Whether the price is just or not can only be ascertained by estimating the cost of production. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCrea) knows the facts. Does he contend that it costs the manufacturers of paper that extra $5,500,000 to produce paper for one year now as compared with what it cost before the war, and that the manufacturers are not making any money at two and a half cents a pound?
Mr. MoCREA: No, they are not making any money. The cost of raw material and of labour have increased very materially. Coal alone is posting us about 100 per cent more, and it requires one ton of coal to make one ton of paper. Coal that used to cost $5 a ton is to-day costing $10 to $11. Fourdrinier wire is a big item of expense. It cost $212 prior to the war, and the life of it was about

five weeks. We figured that out, taking it from the time we started using this material to the time the price increased, and that was the average cost. To-day the cost of the same wire is $490, and the life of the wire is 12 days. The cost of the wire is $490 as against $212 originally.
What accounts for the difference in the life of the wire?

The life of the wire is 12 days as against 5 weeks. The reason for the shorter life of the wire given by the manufacturer is that he cannot get the material. I presume also that he was forced by over production.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend produce, or buy, sulphite?
We buy sulphite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then sulphite enters into your cost?

We make sulphite, but sulphite does not go into newsprint. The sulphite we buy. All the other items have increased in the same proportion. You ask me how it is that we cannot make money now that the price has been increased from 2 cents to 2i cents a pound, or $10 a ton? My reply is that $10 a ton does not begin to meet the additional cost of raw material. Pulp wood alone is selling at twice what it sold for a year ago.

How much do you save by your improved methods?
Mr. MeCREA: We have got it down as low as it can be got by improved methods. Take the case of the International, the largest industry on the continent, having some 30 odd mills; that company has been reorganized two or three times in the last ten years. It had not paid a dividend on its preferred stock up to the time that the increased prices came after the beginning of the war and when the increased prices caused by the War took place it was owing almost an amount equal to 50 per cent of its preferred stock in interest on its preferred stock. The minister said this afternoon that 7 per cent was a fair rate of interest to make on your investment. I agree with him. But, how many factories and industries are there in the country which, during the past ten years, have been obliged to pass their dividends? If it happens now that we are making large profits, if you like, what about the years when we made no profits at all? What about the years when the industries of this country were not able to pay divi-

dends on their preferred stock to say nothing about their common stock? What about the years to come when our industries will probably be very badly crippled?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Supposing we had applied the English method, what would have happened to the pulp and paper industry?
Mr. McCREA; I am not advocating applying the English method.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The English
method is to take the average profits of the three years before the war, and then take 80 per cent of the excess profits over that in time of war.

I am not advocating the English method; I am advocating a common sense method which will apply to everybody equally and alike and under which the rich man will pay according to his means and the poor man will pay also according to his. If you apply that method I am satisfied the people of Canada will be better pleased than they are now. I do not believe there are any people in the country who want to be slackers with regard to paying their fair and legitimate share of the expense of winning this war, rich and poor alike. But, let me finish this question of newsprint. The price of flour to-day is 816 a barrel, wheat 83 a bushel, potatoes $3 to $4 a bushel and pork 17 to 18 cents .live weight. Then, take half fat cattle;
I	saw some sold a short while ago. A farmer drove in a bunch of ten steers weighing about 1,050 apiece and he got $1,150 for the lot or
II	cents a pound live weight. The price of potatoes should only be 75 cents a bushel at the outside; to-day they are $3 to $3.50 a bushel. The price of wheat should not be over 90 cents to $1 a bushel; to-day it is $3 a bushel. The price of flour is $16 a barrel. The minister says that the press of the country must be sustained because it is one of the necessities. If a poor man has a big family and they are crying for bread will they be satisfied with the evening paper? Does it not appeal to the minister that there are other things as well as newsprint that ought to be regulated? The minister says that the winning of the war is the one and the main thing to which we should give our attention but I cannot help thinking that when this delegation from the press came down with their stocking full of printers' ink and told him that they would knock his political head off if he did not listen to them he said: hold
on, gentlemen, 1 do not want to be disfigured that way, I will listen to you; what will you have-paper at 21 cents a pound?-all right, gentlemen, you shall have it; the manufacturer can squeal all he likes but he has got no printers' ink and he cannot hurt me very much with his tongue. I am sorry to believe these things but I leave it to the judgment of the House and the people of the country to say if there is any just reason why the price of newsprint should be fixed at 21 cents a pound, which is one cent less than it can be made for when other branches of business are left untouched. I noticed a short time ago in the Financial Times that a company making sulphite pulp were describing the profits they had made during the last year when the average price was so much; they stated what they expected to make next year when the average price was going to be so much and they ended up by saying that " our business is not affected by the price fixed for newsprint." Why should this condition exist? Why should this one branch of the industry be left so that they could boast that they could make such large profits because they were not affected by what affected another branch of the same industry? I am not jealous of other .people. I wish I could say for the minister and for the Government that they had treated the manufacturers of newsprint as they treated other branches of the industry. I think it would be to the advantage of the Government and for the publishers if that were the case. The publishers are going to suffer for it later on, because they have prevented the construction of additional plants which would have afforded the only remedy for their complaint. If they had patience for about twelve months from the time they started to make the kick, the position would have rectified itself, as there would have been such competition that they could have again dictated the prices as they had done for the past ten years. Simply because we reached a period where for a few months they had to pay an additional price, they .had not the 'foresight to see what would .happen in the future. They made their kick at the wrong time, and will be sorry .for it later on. The American publishers are sorry for it now. They started to fix the price, but they saw where they were going, and thought it best to wait and see what would happen. The Canadian Government would do well, even at this late hour, to change their position, and say to the publishers:	Let supply and demand
govern these things, it is the best regulator

of prices on the face of the earth. And the *minister would be wise to consider well *before imposing additional war taxes on the manufacturers of this country, and see *if he cannot- find some other way of levying taxes so as not to drive capital away *and prevent its investment in Canada. We *who are here will stand it as beet we can, *but the man outside will do as the man to whom you are trying to sell bonds, who *will not buy bonds unless he has some assurance that the bonds will not be loaded down with income tax. The same thing applies to the man with money in his pocket; he will not .invest in a plant in this country unless he has some assurance that it will not be singled out and made to bear the whole burden of the war and other expenses of this country, while other men, equally able to pay, go scot free.
